video.viewing_task:
[14:20] Recall: What financial debt did the British government carry following the Seven Years' War (French and Indian War)?
[22:45] Explain: How did the Boston Massacre of March 1770 become an explosive propaganda victory for Paul Revere and Samuel Adams?
[33:15] Challenge: Why did British ministers in London view colonial resistance as dangerous lawlessness that threatened the entire British constitution?
video.model_answer:
Recall: Britain's national debt had doubled to over £130 million, convincing Parliament that American colonists should help pay for their own military defence.
Explain: Revere's sensationalised engraving depicted British soldiers firing an unprovoked volley into a peaceful crowd of unarmed citizens, turning a chaotic street clash into an enduring symbol of imperial tyranny.
Challenge: London believed in absolute parliamentary sovereignty: if the American colonies were exempt from parliamentary taxation, the authority of the British Crown and the rule of law across the entire empire would collapse.

tasks.title: Chronological Historical Narrative • Analytical Account (3 Paragraphs • 10 mins)
tasks.question: Write a narrative account analysing the key events leading from the Stamp Act (1765) to the Boston Tea Party (1773).
hints: Beginning (1765): Explain how the Stamp Act introduced direct imperial taxation without colonial consent, sparking the rallying cry "No taxation without representation" [4.1].
Middle (1767–1770): Explain how the Townshend Acts and the arrival of British redcoats led directly to street clashes and the Boston Massacre of 1770 [4.2].
End (1773): Explain how Parliament’s 1773 Tea Act granted a monopoly to the East India Company, culminating in the Sons of Liberty dumping 342 chests into Boston Harbour [4.4].

structure_strip: Paragraph 1 (The Initial Breach - 1765 Stamp Act): How British wartime debts prompted taxation and sparked inter-colonial boycotts [4.1].
Paragraph 2 (Rising Violence - 1767–1770): Townshend duties, military occupation of Boston, and the 1770 Boston Massacre [4.2, 4.3].
Paragraph 3 (The Flashpoint - 1773 Boston Tea Party): Sons of Liberty, Dartmouth tea ships, and 342 chests dumped overboard [4.4].
sentence_starters: The conflict began in 1765 when the British Parliament passed the Stamp Act to...
Colonial merchants and assemblies fiercely resisted because...
Following this, tensions escalated sharply when British troops occupied Boston, culminating in...
Although most duties were repealed, Parliament retained the tea duty and passed the 1773 Tea Act to...
Consequently, on the night of 16 December 1773, the Sons of Liberty took decisive action by...

tasks.model_answer:
Initially, colonial anger erupted in December 1773 when the Sons of Liberty dumped 342 chests of British tea into Boston harbour to protest the Tea Act ('No taxation without representation').

In response, Britain passed the harsh 'Intolerable Acts' of 1774, closing Boston port and imposing military rule. The Thirteen Colonies formed the First Continental Congress to coordinate resistance, leading to the first military clashes at Lexington and Concord in April 1775.

Finally, seeing compromise was impossible, the Second Continental Congress adopted Thomas Jefferson’s Declaration of Independence on 4 July 1776, severing all political ties with the British Crown.

lessons.vocab_cloze_text: Deep in debt after 1763, Parliament angered American colonists by enforcing import [Tariff] taxes and the 1765 Stamp Act. Organised by the [Sons of Liberty], merchants launched a coordinated [Boycott] of British goods and condemned troops stationed under [Quartering] rules. After Samuel Adams’s protesters dumped 342 East India Company tea chests into Boston Harbour in December 1773, George III answered with the punitive [Coercive Acts].

stages.title: Lexington, Concord & Dunmore’s Proclamation
stages.trigger: British redcoats clashed with colonial minutemen at Lexington and Concord, while Virginia’s royal governor Lord Dunmore offered freedom to any enslaved person joining the King’s army.
stages.connective: Ignited revolutionary war and terrified American rebel slaveholders, prompting thousands of Black Loyalists to fight for the British Crown.
stages.question: How did fighting at Lexington and Dunmore’s offer widen the war in 1775?

stages.title: The Declaration of Independence & The Slavery Paradox
stages.trigger: Thomas Jefferson drafted the Declaration proclaiming "all men are created equal", while forty-one of the fifty-six rebel signatories were themselves wealthy slaveholders.
stages.connective: Created a profound moral contradiction at the core of the new American Republic that British critics like Dr Samuel Johnson sharply ridiculed.
stages.question: What contradiction lay behind Jefferson’s 1776 claim of equal rights?

stages.title: Saratoga & The French Global Intervention
stages.trigger: The American victory at Saratoga convinced France, Spain, and the Dutch Republic to join the war, deploying battle fleets to threaten British Caribbean sugar islands.
stages.connective: Stretched the Royal Navy thin across the globe, preventing Britain from concentrating its military forces exclusively on North America.
stages.question: How did victory at Saratoga in 1777 turn the war into a global clash?

stages.title: The Siege of Yorktown & British Surrender
stages.trigger: Admiral de Grasse’s French fleet won the Battle of the Chesapeake, trapping General Cornwallis on the Yorktown peninsula without naval rescue until he surrendered.
stages.connective: Shattered Britain’s political will to continue fighting, forcing Parliament to open peace negotiations and accept American independence.
stages.question: How did Washington and French warships trap Cornwallis at Yorktown?

stages.title: The Treaty of Paris & The Black Loyalist Exodus
stages.trigger: The Treaty of Paris recognized American independence, while British Commander Sir Guy Carleton refused George Washington’s demands and evacuated 3,000 Black Loyalists to Nova Scotia.
stages.connective: Marked the dramatic collapse of the First British Empire in the Atlantic, turning Britain’s imperial attention eastward toward India and the Pacific.
stages.question: What happened to the 3,000 Black Loyalists after the 1783 Paris treaty?

lessons.did_you_know: When Thomas Jefferson drafted the famous words "All men are created equal, endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable Rights", he personally owned over 170 enslaved human beings at his Monticello estate and never freed them! Meanwhile, the British Royal Governor of Virginia, Lord Dunmore, issued a proclamation offering immediate freedom to any enslaved person who escaped rebel owners and joined the British Army—leading 20,000 enslaved Africans to risk their lives fleeing to British lines wearing badges reading "Liberty to Slaves"!

items.question: How large was Great Britain’s imperial war debt following victory in the Seven Years’ War in 1763?
items.explanation: Winning the global Seven Years’ War left Great Britain burdened with an enormous £133 million national debt in 1763.

items.question: Which 1765 parliamentary law taxed colonial legal documents, newspapers, pamphlets, and playing cards?
items.explanation: Passed in 1765 to raise colonial revenue, the Stamp Act placed direct taxes on printed paper goods and legal documents.

items.question: On what date did British soldiers fire into a crowd on Boston’s icy King Street during the Boston Massacre?
items.explanation: On 5 March 1770, panicked British redcoats fired on a hostile crowd on King Street in Boston.

items.question: Which May 1773 parliamentary law granted the East India Company a monopoly to sell tea directly to American ports?
items.explanation: In May 1773, Parliament enacted the Tea Act to rescue the financially troubled East India Company.

items.question: How did Sons of Liberty protesters disguise themselves when boarding tea ships in Boston Harbour on 16 December 1773?
items.answer: Disguised as Mohawks with war paint and blankets
items.explanation: On the night of 16 December 1773, Sons of Liberty members disguised themselves as Mohawks to board three British tea ships.

items.question: Which 1763 royal decree issued by King George III forbade white colonists from settling west of the Appalachian Mountains?
items.explanation: King George III issued the Proclamation Line of 1763 to prevent costly frontier wars with Native American nations.

items.question: What constitutional grievance did colonists proclaim in opposition to the 1765 Stamp Act?
items.explanation: Colonists declared that taxation without elected representation in Westminster violated their rights as freeborn Englishmen.

items.question: How many colonists were killed when British redcoats discharged their muskets during the Boston Massacre?
items.explanation: Five colonists were killed on the cobbles of King Street during the clash on 5 March 1770.

items.question: How much unsold surplus tea was sitting in East India Company warehouses in London prior to the May 1773 Tea Act?
items.explanation: The East India Company held 18 million pounds of unsold tea in London warehouses when Parliament passed the Tea Act.

items.question: How many chests of East India Company tea were smashed open and emptied into Boston Harbour on 16 December 1773?
items.explanation: In three disciplined hours, protesters smashed open 342 chests of tea and dumped them into Boston Harbour.

vocab.definition: A formal, binding public announcement declaring a fundamental political decision or the birth of a nation.
Fundamental human rights (such as life, liberty, and happiness) that cannot be taken away or surrendered to any government.
An enslaved African who escaped rebel masters to fight for the British Crown in exchange for guaranteed freedom.
The supreme, independent authority of a state to govern itself free from outside foreign control.
A military force raised from the civilian population to supplement a regular army in times of emergency.
The 1783 peace agreement in which Great Britain formally recognised the independence of the United States of America.
Claiming to have moral principles or beliefs to which one’s own actual behaviour and actions do not conform.
A person appointed to administer a country because the monarch is a minor, absent, or incapacitated.
The entry of foreign military powers (such as France and Spain) into a conflict to aid one of the warring sides.
The organised withdrawal of troops, military personnel, or refugees from a dangerous or defeated territory.

narrative_blocks.title: The Shot Heard ’Round the World: Lexington & Concord (April 1775)
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.1] In April 1775, British redcoats marched to seize colonial munitions at Concord. The famous Paul Revere midnight alarm warned town militias to mobilize, leading to an armed standoff at Lexington Green where someone fired the shot heard round the world.

As war spread, Virginia’s royal governor issued Dunmore’s freedom offer, promising emancipation to enslaved Black laborers who fled rebel plantations to bear arms for King George III, prompting thousands to join the British forces.

source.title: Source A (Strategic Emancipation): Lord Dunmore's Proclamation of Freedom to Enslaved Persons (November 1775)
source.caption: Official broadside issued by John Murray, 4th Earl of Dunmore, Royal Governor of Virginia, offering freedom to all enslaved persons belonging to rebels who agreed to fight for the British Crown.
source.citation: Library of Virginia, Richmond (Broadside 1775 .M87) / The National Archives, Kew (CO 5/1353).
source.provenance: Printed aboard the British merchant ship William off Norfolk, Virginia on 7 November 1775.
source.context: Facing armed rebellion in Virginia, Lord Dunmore issued an ultimatum declaring martial law and offering freedom to enslaved men who joined the British Army. Over 800 African Americans joined his 'Ethiopian Regiment' wearing sashes reading 'Liberty to Slaves'. **Hinge Question:** Did Lord Dunmore issue his proclamation out of genuine humanitarian concern for enslaved Africans or as a cynical military weapon?

utility_enquiry.question: Why did Virginia's royal governor Lord Dunmore promise freedom to enslaved Africans who fled to join the British forces?
utility_enquiry.model_answer: Dunmore sought to cripple the Virginia plantation economy and bolster his outnumbered British forces by encouraging thousands of enslaved workers to abandon rebel masters and bear arms for the King.
utility_enquiry.content_inferences: Demonstrates how enslaved people actively leveraged the imperial conflict to claim their own freedom, transforming the war into a war of liberation.
utility_enquiry.provenance_evaluation: Official royal proclamation and military tactic; deliberately targeted only the property of rebel colonists while protecting loyalist enslavers.
utility_enquiry.context_limitations: Reflects military desperation rather than moral abolitionism; Dunmore personally owned enslaved people and returned loyalists' slaves.

narrative_blocks.title: The 1776 Declaration & The Paradox of Liberty (July 1776)
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.2] In July 1776, the Continental Congress in Philadelphia met to adopt the Declaration of Independence. Drafting the historic text with Jefferson’s eagle quill, Thomas Jefferson wrote the immortal words declaring that all men created equal with natural rights to life and liberty.

Yet the founding document concealed a profound moral hypocrisy: forty-one of the fifty-six slaveholder signatories personally owned enslaved humans, deliberately denying basic legal and human freedom to half a million African Americans across the colonies.

source.title: Source B (Revolutionary Discourse): Thomas Paine's Common Sense Title Page (Philadelphia, January 1776)
source.caption: Title page of the first edition of Thomas Paine's explosive political pamphlet Common Sense, published anonymously in Philadelphia on 10 January 1776.
source.citation: Library of Congress, Rare Book and Special Collections Division (Call number: E211 .P145 1776).
source.provenance: Published anonymously in Philadelphia by printer Robert Bell in January 1776.
source.context: Before Common Sense, most colonists claimed they were only fighting for their traditional rights as British subjects. Paine demolished the divine right of kings, ridiculed the British monarchy, and argued that America had a moral duty to create an independent democratic republic. **Hinge Question:** What made Thomas Paine's writing style so revolutionary compared to the formal legal petitions previously sent to the King?
source.question: Why was Thomas Paine's pamphlet Common Sense so uniquely persuasive in convincing ordinary colonists to demand total independence?
source.hinge_question: What made Thomas Paine's writing style so revolutionary compared to the formal legal petitions previously sent to the King?

utility_enquiry.question: Why was Thomas Paine's pamphlet Common Sense so uniquely persuasive in convincing ordinary colonists to demand total independence?
utility_enquiry.model_answer: Written in vigorous, accessible, plain English avoiding elite Latin phrases, Paine attacked hereditary monarchy as absurd and argued that it was common sense for an entire continent not to be ruled by a distant island.
utility_enquiry.content_inferences: Illustrates the power of print culture in transforming elite constitutional debates into a mass popular revolution.
utility_enquiry.provenance_evaluation: A revolutionary political manifesto designed for wide circulation; sold over 150,000 copies in a population of 2.5 million.
utility_enquiry.context_limitations: An impassioned polemic that caricatures British institutions to persuade readers, rather than an objective analysis of imperial governance.

bullet_points.label: Demystifying Monarchy
bullet_points.text: Paine called King George III 'the Royal Brute of Britain', breaking the psychological reverence ordinary colonists held for the Crown.

bullet_points.label: Vision of Global Democracy
bullet_points.text: He framed America as 'an asylum for mankind', arguing that independence was not just a colonial dispute but a world-changing birth of freedom.

narrative_blocks.title: Thomas Paine’s Common Sense & The Global Alliance (1776–1778)
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.3] The decisive turning point arrived in October 1777 at Saratoga, where American continental forces triumphed by defeating General Burgoyne. This victory convinced King Louis XVI warships and French armies to enter the conflict as formal military allies of the American rebels.

The conflict transformed rapidly into a global war. Great Britain suffered severe sugar island divergence, compelled to divert vital warships away from North America to safeguard its fabulously lucrative Caribbean sugar colonies against French capture.

source.title: Source C (Enlightenment Ideology): Declaration of Independence (John Trumbull, 4 July 1776)
source.caption: Monumental oil painting by John Trumbull depicting the Committee of Five (John Adams, Roger Sherman, Robert Livingston, Thomas Jefferson, and Benjamin Franklin) presenting the draft Declaration of Independence to John Hancock.
source.citation: United States Capitol Rotunda, Washington, D.C. Oil on canvas by John Trumbull, 1818.
source.provenance: Commissioned by the United States Congress in 1817 to commemorate the founding constitutional act of the republic.
source.context: On 4 July 1776, the Continental Congress voted to approve the Declaration of Independence. Jefferson's preamble asserted that all men possess unalienable rights to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. **Hinge Question:** How did Thomas Jefferson reconcile writing that 'all men are created equal' while personally enslaving over 600 human beings?
source.question: How does John Trumbull's painting celebrate the Committee of Five presenting the Declaration of Independence to the Continental Congress?
source.hinge_question: How did Thomas Jefferson reconcile writing that 'all men are created equal' while personally enslaving over 600 human beings?

utility_enquiry.question: How does John Trumbull's painting celebrate the Committee of Five presenting the Declaration of Independence to the Continental Congress?
utility_enquiry.model_answer: It frames the moment as an orderly, dignified gathering of rational republican statesmen, emphasizing moral courage and philosophical resolve over revolutionary violence.
utility_enquiry.content_inferences: Portrays the birth of the American republic as a noble Enlightenment act of civic courage and legal deliberation.
utility_enquiry.provenance_evaluation: Monumental patriotic painting displayed in the heart of the US Capitol; designed to establish a sacred national visual mythology.
utility_enquiry.context_limitations: An artistic dramatization painted 40 years later; the 47 delegates depicted were never assembled in the room simultaneously on 4 July.

bullet_points.label: Universal Principles of Freedom
bullet_points.text: The painting glorifies the adoption of natural rights philosophy, declaring that governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed.

bullet_points.label: Racial and Gender Exclusions
bullet_points.text: The all-white, all-male assembly visualizes the historic paradox of a revolution fighting for liberty while entrenching chattel slavery and excluding women.

provenance_clues: Author: John Trumbull, American painter and former aide-de-camp to General George Washington.
Audience: The citizens of the United States and international visitors to the US Capitol.
Motive: To preserve the likenesses of the founding fathers and instill national reverence for the Declaration.

narrative_blocks.heading: Thomas Paine’s Common Sense & The Global Alliance (1776–1778)
narrative_blocks.content:
[5.3] The decisive turning point arrived in October 1777 at Saratoga, where American continental forces triumphed by defeating General Burgoyne. This victory convinced King Louis XVI warships and French armies to enter the conflict as formal military allies of the American rebels.

The conflict transformed rapidly into a global war. Great Britain suffered severe sugar island divergence, compelled to divert vital warships away from North America to safeguard its fabulously lucrative Caribbean sugar colonies against French capture.

narrative_blocks.title: Siege of Yorktown & British Surrender (October 1781)
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.4] In autumn 1781, British commander Lord Cornwallis marched into a peninsula trap at Yorktown, Virginia. George Washington’s forces besieged the garrison by land, while French Admiral de Grasse Chesapeake blockade cut off all British naval reinforcements and rescue.

Trapped and relentlessly pounded by heavy artillery, Cornwallis surrendered eight thousand redcoats on 19 October 1781. As defeated British soldiers marched out to lay down their muskets, their military band famously played the melancholy ballad The World Turned Upside Down.

narrative_blocks.caption: John Trumbull's oil painting 'Surrender of Lord Cornwallis' at Yorktown, Virginia (19 October 1781), showing American and French armies surrounding British forces.

source.title: Source D (Documentary Emancipation): The Book of Negroes: Inspection Certificate Signed by Samuel Birch (1783)
source.caption: Official military pass and registration entry from The Book of Negroes, certifying that an emancipated Black Loyalist had been inspected and cleared to board a British evacuation vessel in New York Harbor.
source.citation: The National Archives, Kew (PRO 30/55/100, Carleton Papers) / Library and Archives Canada.
source.provenance: Compiled in New York City between April and November 1783 by a joint British-American inspection commission.
source.context: At the end of the Revolutionary War, George Washington demanded that all runaway slaves within British lines be returned to their American masters. British Commander-in-Chief Sir Guy Carleton refused, declaring it an insult to British honor, and created The Book of Negroes to evacuate 3,000 Black Loyalists to Nova Scotia. **Hinge Question:** Why did thousands of African Americans choose to fight for the British King rather than the American Patriots who claimed to be fighting for 'liberty'?
source.question: What does the meticulous documentation in The Book of Negroes reveal about the British evacuation of Black Loyalists from New York in 1783?
source.hinge_question: Why did thousands of African Americans choose to fight for the British King rather than the American Patriots who claimed to be fighting for 'liberty'?

utility_enquiry.question: What does the meticulous documentation in The Book of Negroes reveal about the British evacuation of Black Loyalists from New York in 1783?
utility_enquiry.model_answer: It records the names, ages, physical descriptions, and former enslavers of over 3,000 formerly enslaved African Americans, proving that the British military honored its pledge of freedom and protected them from re-enslavement.
utility_enquiry.content_inferences: Provides invaluable biographical evidence of ordinary African Americans seizing freedom through military alliance with the British Crown.
utility_enquiry.provenance_evaluation: Official military legal ledger signed by British officers; created to satisfy American property claims while ensuring Black Loyalists sailed away free.
utility_enquiry.context_limitations: Documents the successful escapees, but cannot capture the thousands of Black Loyalists who were recaptured by slave patrols, died of smallpox, or were abandoned in the South.

bullet_points.text: General Carleton insisted that returning men who had shed blood for the King back into slavery was a moral impossibility.

bullet_points.label: Founding the Black Loyalist Diaspora
bullet_points.text: Those evacuated in The Book of Negroes founded free Black communities in Birchtown, Nova Scotia, and later Sierra Leone (Freetown).

narrative_blocks.title: The Treaty of Paris & The Black Loyalists (1783)
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.5] In September 1783, the American independence treaty signed at Paris recognized the United States as a sovereign republic. In New York, British commander Sir Guy Carleton protected three thousand Black Loyalists who had loyally served the British Crown during the war.

British military clerks registered their names into Book of Negroes ledgers, issuing freedom certificates that allowed families to board Nova Scotia evacuation ships, securing liberty in Canada and later founding Freetown in Sierra Leone.

source.title: Source E (Diplomatic Settlement & Peace): The Treaty of Paris: Signatures and Wax Seals Page (3 September 1783)
source.caption: Official concluding page of the definitive Treaty of Paris, displaying the signatures and red wax seals of British envoy David Hartley and American commissioners John Adams, Benjamin Franklin, and John Jay.
source.citation: US National Archives and Records Administration, Washington, D.C. (Record Group 11, Exchange Copy).
source.provenance: Signed at the Hotel d'York in Paris on 3 September 1783, bringing formal conclusion to the American Revolutionary War.
source.context: Signed in Paris in September 1783, the treaty ended eight years of war. Britain formally recognized the United States as independent and ceded all territory from the Atlantic to the Mississippi, marking the catastrophic collapse of the First British Empire. **Hinge Question:** Why was Great Britain willing to grant such vast western lands to its former colonies despite having undefeated garrisons in New York and Charleston?
source.question: What immense territorial and political concessions did Great Britain make in the 1783 Treaty of Paris?
source.hinge_question: Why was Great Britain willing to grant such vast western lands to its former colonies despite having undefeated garrisons in New York and Charleston?

utility_enquiry.question: What immense territorial and political concessions did Great Britain make in the 1783 Treaty of Paris?
utility_enquiry.model_answer: Britain formally recognized the United States as free, sovereign, and independent nations, ceding all imperial territory between the Atlantic Ocean and the Mississippi River from Canada to Florida.
utility_enquiry.content_inferences: Documents the legal dissolution of the First British Empire in North America and the emergence of a new sovereign transcontinental power.
utility_enquiry.provenance_evaluation: Premier international diplomatic treaty binding under global law; signed with official wax seals by the chief peace plenipotentiaries.
utility_enquiry.context_limitations: While granting western lands to the Americans, the treaty completely excluded Native American tribes who actually inhabited those territories.

bullet_points.text: Article 1 formally declared the United States to be free, sovereign, and independent, relinquishing all Crown claims to government and territorial property.

bullet_points.label: Vast Territorial Cession
bullet_points.text: Britain ceded all land west to the Mississippi River, doubling American territory and shutting out Native American allies from peace discussions.

Motive: To establish permanent peace, settle borders, and restore commercial relations between Britain and the United States.

sources.title: Source A (Strategic Emancipation): Lord Dunmore's Proclamation of Freedom to Enslaved Persons (November 1775)
sources.caption: Official broadside issued by John Murray, 4th Earl of Dunmore, Royal Governor of Virginia, offering freedom to all enslaved persons belonging to rebels who agreed to fight for the British Crown.
sources.citation: Library of Virginia, Richmond (Broadside 1775 .M87) / The National Archives, Kew (CO 5/1353).
sources.provenance: Printed aboard the British merchant ship William off Norfolk, Virginia on 7 November 1775.
sources.context: Facing armed rebellion in Virginia, Lord Dunmore issued an ultimatum declaring martial law and offering freedom to enslaved men who joined the British Army. Over 800 African Americans joined his 'Ethiopian Regiment' wearing sashes reading 'Liberty to Slaves'. **Hinge Question:** Did Lord Dunmore issue his proclamation out of genuine humanitarian concern for enslaved Africans or as a cynical military weapon?
sources.question: Why did Virginia's royal governor Lord Dunmore promise freedom to enslaved Africans who fled to join the British forces?
sources.hinge_question: Did Lord Dunmore issue his proclamation out of genuine humanitarian concern for enslaved Africans or as a cynical military weapon?

utility_enquiry.question: Why did Virginia's royal governor Lord Dunmore promise freedom to enslaved Africans who fled to join the British forces?
utility_enquiry.model_answer: Dunmore sought to cripple the Virginia plantation economy and bolster his outnumbered British forces by encouraging thousands of enslaved workers to abandon rebel masters and bear arms for the King.
utility_enquiry.content_inferences: Demonstrates how enslaved people actively leveraged the imperial conflict to claim their own freedom, transforming the war into a war of liberation.
utility_enquiry.provenance_evaluation: Official royal proclamation and military tactic; deliberately targeted only the property of rebel colonists while protecting loyalist enslavers.
utility_enquiry.context_limitations: Reflects military desperation rather than moral abolitionism; Dunmore personally owned enslaved people and returned loyalists' slaves.

bullet_points.label: Economic Disruption
bullet_points.text: Dunmore knew that the threat of slave insurrections would force rebel planters to abandon the Continental Army to guard their plantations.

bullet_points.label: Black Loyalist Mobilisation
bullet_points.text: Thousands of enslaved men and women escaped to British lines, serving as armed soldiers, guides, sailors, and military laborers throughout the war.

Motive: To suppress the colonial rebellion through economic disruption and recruit an 'Ethiopian Regiment' of Black Loyalists.

sources.title: Source B (Revolutionary Discourse): Thomas Paine's Common Sense Title Page (Philadelphia, January 1776)
sources.caption: Title page of the first edition of Thomas Paine's explosive political pamphlet Common Sense, published anonymously in Philadelphia on 10 January 1776.
sources.citation: Library of Congress, Rare Book and Special Collections Division (Call number: E211 .P145 1776).
sources.provenance: Published anonymously in Philadelphia by printer Robert Bell in January 1776.
sources.context: Before Common Sense, most colonists claimed they were only fighting for their traditional rights as British subjects. Paine demolished the divine right of kings, ridiculed the British monarchy, and argued that America had a moral duty to create an independent democratic republic. **Hinge Question:** What made Thomas Paine's writing style so revolutionary compared to the formal legal petitions previously sent to the King?
sources.question: Why was Thomas Paine's pamphlet Common Sense so uniquely persuasive in convincing ordinary colonists to demand total independence?
sources.hinge_question: What made Thomas Paine's writing style so revolutionary compared to the formal legal petitions previously sent to the King?

utility_enquiry.question: Why was Thomas Paine's pamphlet Common Sense so uniquely persuasive in convincing ordinary colonists to demand total independence?
utility_enquiry.model_answer: Written in vigorous, accessible, plain English avoiding elite Latin phrases, Paine attacked hereditary monarchy as absurd and argued that it was common sense for an entire continent not to be ruled by a distant island.
utility_enquiry.content_inferences: Illustrates the power of print culture in transforming elite constitutional debates into a mass popular revolution.
utility_enquiry.provenance_evaluation: A revolutionary political manifesto designed for wide circulation; sold over 150,000 copies in a population of 2.5 million.
utility_enquiry.context_limitations: An impassioned polemic that caricatures British institutions to persuade readers, rather than an objective analysis of imperial governance.

bullet_points.label: Demystifying Monarchy
bullet_points.text: Paine called King George III 'the Royal Brute of Britain', breaking the psychological reverence ordinary colonists held for the Crown.

bullet_points.label: Vision of Global Democracy
bullet_points.text: He framed America as 'an asylum for mankind', arguing that independence was not just a colonial dispute but a world-changing birth of freedom.

Motive: To transform a colonial tax protest into an uncompromising moral campaign for universal human liberty and republican independence.

lessons.prologue: In July 1776, American delegates proclaimed that 'all men are created equal' and declared independence from King George III. Yet thousands of enslaved Black Loyalists fled to British battle-lines, seeking genuine personal freedom under the Crown. At Yorktown in 1781, Britain surrendered. How did revolutionary ideals collide with imperial defeat and the reality of slavery?

tasks.question: ‘British defeat in the American Revolutionary War was caused primarily by French naval intervention rather than American military strength.’ How far do you agree?
stimulus: George Washington and the Continental Army’s strategy of survival
French naval intervention and the Battle of the Chesapeake (1781)
hints: Point: Assess how French naval intervention cut off British army resupply at Yorktown in 1781 [5.4].
Evidence: Cite Admiral de Grasse blockading Chesapeake Bay and Rochambeau’s ground troops trapping General Cornwallis.
Explanation: Contrast this with Washington’s defensive strategy and the victory at Saratoga (1777) that convinced France to enter the war [5.2, 5.3].
Link: Reach a balanced conclusion evaluating whether French naval power or American persistence was the decisive factor.

structure_strip: PEEL 1 (French Naval Intervention): Explain how Admiral de Grasse’s fleet trapped Cornwallis at Yorktown in 1781, preventing Royal Navy evacuation [5.4].
PEEL 2 (American Military Resilience): Explain how Washington kept the Continental Army intact, won at Saratoga, and utilized local militia knowledge [5.2, 5.3].
PEEL 3 (British Strategic Failures): Explain how vast transatlantic supply lines and hostile local populations made British reconquest impossible [5.1].
Conclusion: Provide an evaluative judgment weighing which factor was truly decisive.
sentence_starters: One decisive reason was that French naval intervention was the decisive factor because...
At the Siege of Yorktown in 1781, Admiral de Grasse’s fleet succeeded in...
On the other hand, American military persistence under George Washington was essential because...
Furthermore, the American victory at Saratoga (1777) was critical as it...
Additionally, Britain suffered from insurmountable logistical weaknesses, including...
In conclusion, while American resilience sustained the war, French naval intervention was decisive because...
connective_bank: A compelling argument supporting this statement is that...

tasks.model_answer:
On the one hand, French military and naval intervention was the decisive turning point in securing American independence. Following the crucial American victory at Saratoga (1777), France formed an official military alliance with the United States in 1778, providing vital naval fleets, professional troops under General Rochambeau, and massive financial loans. Most crucially, at the Siege of Yorktown in 1781, Admiral de Grasse’s French fleet won the Battle of the Chesapeake, blockading British reinforcements by sea while Franco-American armies encircled General Cornwallis on land, forcing the final British surrender.

On the other hand, British strategic blunders and geographical distance were equally fundamental causes of the American victory. The British military faced the insurmountable logistical challenge of supplying armies across 3,000 miles of the Atlantic Ocean against a decentralized enemy with no single capital to capture. Furthermore, George Washington’s Fabian strategy of calculated retreat kept the Continental Army intact while local colonial militias waged effective guerrilla warfare. Therefore, while French naval power delivered the final blow at Yorktown, British strategic isolation in a vast, hostile continent made sustaining colonial rule impossible.

key_individuals.name: The East India Company (EIC)
key_individuals.role: Joint-Stock Trading Monopoly That Became Territorial Ruler of Bengal
key_individuals.origins: Granted a royal monopoly charter by Queen Elizabeth I on New Year’s Eve 1600 after 218 London merchants pooled £68,000 for James Lancaster’s spice voyage (earning 300%+ profits).
key_individuals.significance: Grew from fortified coastal warehouses ("factories" at Surat, Madras, Bombay, and Calcutta) guarded by sepoy infantry into a private corporate empire collecting taxes over 20 million people in Bengal after 1765—whose unbending revenue demands worsened the catastrophic 1770 Bengal Famine (10 million deaths) and whose 1773 Tea Act sparked the Boston Tea Party.
achievements: Established fortified trading factories across Mughal coastlines following Sir Thomas Roe’s 1615–19 embassy to Emperor Jahangir.
Defeated Nawab Siraj ud-Daulah at Plassey (1757) and acquired the sovereign Diwani tax-collection right across Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa under the 1765 Treaty of Allahabad.
Granted a direct colonial tea monopoly under Parliament’s May 1773 Tea Act to clear 18 million pounds of unsold London tea, triggering the December 1773 Boston Tea Party.

key_individuals.name: Sir Thomas Roe
key_individuals.role: English Royal Ambassador to the Mughal Court of Emperor Jahangir (1615–1619)
key_individuals.origins: English diplomat dispatched by King James I in 1615 to the fabulously wealthy court of Mughal Emperor Jahangir when Mughal India produced over a quarter of global manufacturing.
key_individuals.significance: Negotiated imperial permission (farman) for English merchants to establish permanent trading "factories" at Surat—marking the peaceful, deferential commercial phase of Anglo-Mughal relations a century and a half before Plassey.
achievements: Attended Emperor Jahangir’s court (1615–19) as official ambassador of King James I.
Secured Mughal authorisation for fortified English warehouse depots at Surat in exchange for European silver bullion and novelties.

key_individuals.name: Nawab Siraj ud-Daulah
key_individuals.role: Last Independent Nawab of Bengal (1756–1757)
key_individuals.origins: Twenty-three-year-old ruler of wealthy Mughal Bengal who ordered the East India Company in 1756 to stop mounting unauthorised heavy cannons around Fort William in Calcutta.
key_individuals.significance: Captured Fort William with 50,000 troops in June 1756 (followed by the "Black Hole" guardroom deaths sensationalised in Britain), before being overthrown at the Battle of Plassey on 23 June 1757 when his general Mir Jafar accepted Robert Clive’s secret bribes.
achievements: Marched 50,000 soldiers to seize Calcutta’s Fort William (1756) to defend Bengali sovereignty against illegal Company fortifications.
Betrayed at Plassey (23 June 1757) when Mir Jafar held Bengal’s main divisions motionless and monsoon rain soaked Siraj’s uncovered cannon powder.

key_individuals.name: Robert Clive (1st Baron Clive)
key_individuals.role: East India Company Commander & Architect of Company Rule in Bengal
key_individuals.origins: Ambitious East India Company officer dispatched to recapture Calcutta in 1757, who combined military calculation with secret political bribery.
key_individuals.significance: Bribed Bengali commander Mir Jafar to win the Battle of Plassey (23 June 1757) and forced defeated Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II to sign the August 1765 Treaty of Allahabad—handing the Company the Diwani tax revenues of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa.
achievements: Used secret gold promises and tarpaulin-shielded artillery during a monsoon storm to defeat Siraj ud-Daulah at Plassey (23 June 1757) and install Mir Jafar as puppet Nawab.
Secured the 1765 Treaty of Allahabad from Emperor Shah Alam II, turning a London trading company into a territorial tax-collecting state.

key_individuals.name: The Royal African Company (RAC)
key_individuals.role: Stuart Royal Slave-Trading Monopoly on the West African Coast
key_individuals.origins: Chartered by King Charles II in 1672 and headed by his brother James, Duke of York, to monopolise English trafficking along the West African coast within the Atlantic Triangular Trade.
key_individuals.significance: Demonstrated direct Stuart Crown and City involvement in transatlantic chattel slavery—imprisoning kidnapped Africans in fortified coastal dungeons (headquartered at Cape Coast Castle), branding captives "RAC" on the chest, and shipping tens of thousands across the deadly eight-week Middle Passage (where roughly one in six died, alongside atrocities such as the 1781 Zong massacre of 133 captives).
achievements: Operated armed West African slave forts exchanging British guns, iron bars, brass pans, and textiles for human captives.
Paved the way for Britain’s 1713 Spanish Asiento contract making Liverpool and Bristol Europe’s dominant slave-trading ports.

key_individuals.name: Olaudah Equiano
key_individuals.role: Freed African Author & Leading British Abolitionist Campaigner
key_individuals.origins: Enslaved as a boy in West Africa, carried across the Middle Passage, and later able to purchase his freedom through maritime trade before settling in London as a prominent voice in the Sons of Africa.
key_individuals.significance: Published his bestselling 1789 autobiography The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano—providing powerful firsthand African testimony alongside the 1788 Brookes ship diagram, Granville Sharp’s exposure of the 1781 Zong case, and Josiah Wedgwood’s medallion to propel Parliament toward the 1807 Abolition of the Slave Trade Act.
achievements: Published nine editions of his bestselling 1789 autobiography during his lifetime and toured Britain lecturing against the slave trade.
Helped transform British public opinion ahead of the landmark Abolition Act of 1807.

key_individuals.name: Queen Nanny of the Maroons
key_individuals.role: Asante Military & Spiritual Leader of the Windward Jamaican Maroons
key_individuals.origins: Leader of self-liberated Windward Maroon communities in Jamaica’s rugged Blue Mountains after Africans escaped Spanish and British sugar plantations following Cromwell’s 1655 seizure of Jamaica.
key_individuals.significance: Defeated heavily armed British regiments using forest leaf camouflage, cow-horn abeng signals, and mountain guerrilla ambushes—forcing British Governor Edward Trelawny to sign the 1739 Maroon peace treaties recognizing Maroon freedom and 1,500 sovereign acres.
achievements: Trained Maroon fighters in living-branch camouflage, abeng horn communication, and mountain ambush warfare alongside communal crop farming.
Forced Britain to negotiate the 1739 peace treaties acknowledging Maroon liberty and land (albeit containing the painful clause requiring Maroons to return future plantation runaways).

key_individuals.name: King George III
key_individuals.role: British Monarch During the Loss of the Thirteen American Colonies (1760–1820)
key_individuals.origins: Crowned in 1760 near the close of the Seven Years’ War, which left Great Britain victorious over France yet burdened with an enormous £133 million imperial war debt.
key_individuals.significance: Issued the Royal Proclamation of 1763 barring colonial settlement west of the Appalachians and backed parliamentary colonial taxation (1765 Stamp Act, 1773 Tea Act) and the punitive 1774 Coercive Acts after the Boston Tea Party—driving the Thirteen Colonies into the 1775–83 War of Independence.
achievements: Established the 1763 Proclamation Line and supported Quartering Acts and colonial duties to pay Seven Years’ War debts.

Responded to the 16 December 1773 destruction of 342 tea chests (£10,000) in Boston Harbour with the 1774 Coercive Acts closing Boston Port, culminating in British defeat at Saratoga (1777) and Yorktown (1781) and the 1783 Treaty of Paris.

key_individuals.name: Thomas Jefferson & George Washington
key_individuals.role: Author of the 1776 Declaration of Independence & Continental Army Commander
key_individuals.origins: Virginian Patriot leaders who challenged British "taxation without representation" after Lexington (April 1775) and Thomas Paine’s Common Sense (January 1776)—while both personally enslaving hundreds of African Americans.
key_individuals.significance: Jefferson drafted the July 1776 Declaration of Independence proclaiming "all men are created equal" (despite 41 of 56 signatories owning enslaved people), and Washington—aided by King Louis XVI’s French fleet after Saratoga (1777)—besieged Lord Cornwallis at Yorktown on 19 October 1781 to win US independence in 1783.
achievements: Jefferson authored the 4 July 1776 Declaration of Independence asserting natural rights to life and liberty while leaving chattel slavery intact.
Washington trapped 8,000 British regulars under Lord Cornwallis at Yorktown (October 1781) alongside French Admiral de Grasse’s Chesapeake naval blockade.

key_individuals.name: Lord Dunmore’s Ethiopian Regiment & The Black Loyalists
key_individuals.role: Enslaved African Americans Who Fought for the British Crown to Win Freedom
key_individuals.origins: Launched in November 1775 when Virginia’s Royal Governor Lord Dunmore issued a proclamation promising freedom to Patriot-owned enslaved people who crossed British lines to bear arms for King George III.
key_individuals.significance: Exposed the stark paradox of the American Revolution: thousands of enslaved men and women sought liberty with the British Army, and in 1783 British commander Sir Guy Carleton registered 3,000 Black Loyalists in the Book of Negroes at New York to sail free to Nova Scotia (and later found Freetown, Sierra Leone).
achievements: Thousands escaped rebel plantations following Lord Dunmore’s November 1775 Proclamation and later British emancipation promises.
In 1783, 3,000 Black Loyalists received British freedom certificates ("Birch Certificates") recorded in the Book of Negroes and evacuated from New York to Nova Scotia.

guided_reading.book_title: Sir Thomas Roe’s Embassy Journal at the Mughal Court & Clive’s Diwani Letter (1616–1765)
guided_reading.author: Sir Thomas Roe (1616, BL Add MS 6115) & Robert Clive to EIC Directors (30 Sept 1765)
guided_reading.cover_caption: Michiel Jansz. van Mierevelt (after), Portrait of Sir Thomas Roe (c. 1640, National Portrait Gallery), English ambassador to Mughal Emperor Jahangir.
guided_reading.author_context: When English merchants first arrived in South Asia after 1600, Mughal India produced roughly a quarter of the entire world’s manufactured goods. Comparing Ambassador Sir Thomas Roe’s humble petitioning at Emperor Jahangir’s court in 1616 with Robert Clive’s triumphant 1765 dispatch to London after Plassey and the Treaty of Allahabad reveals how a trading company turned itself into a territorial tax-collecting empire.
guided_reading.extract:
From Sir Thomas Roe’s Journal and Letter to the East India Company from the Court of Emperor Jahangir at Ajmer (1616): "Let this be received as a rule: that if you will profit, seek it at sea, and in quiet trade; for without controversy it is an error to affect garrisons and land wars in India. The Great Mogul commands revenues and horsemen beyond any prince of Christendom; our humble factories at Surat exist solely by his imperial firman [decree] and pleasure."

One hundred and forty-nine years later, after Mughal imperial power fragmented and East India Company sepoy armies seized Bengal at Plassey (1757) and Buxar (1764), Robert Clive wrote to the Court of Directors in London on 30 September 1765 announcing the Treaty of Allahabad: "We have at last arrived at that critical period which I have long foreseen... By the Emperor Shah Alam’s grant of the Diwani, your Company are now become the sovereigns of a rich and potent kingdom. All the revenues of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa—amounting after tribute to above two millions sterling clear per annum—will henceforth pass into your treasury, paying for our armies and our China and Indian cargoes without sending an ounce of silver from England."

vocabVault.def: An official imperial decree issued by the Mughal Emperor granting trading privileges or customs exemptions.
A corporate business—like the East India Company (chartered 1600)—funded by shareholders who shared trading profits.
Indian infantry soldiers recruited, drilled, and paid by the East India Company with European muskets and artillery.
The Treaty of Allahabad’s transfer of the right to collect land taxes across Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa (~20 million people) to the East India Company.

parent_discussion.question: In 1616, why did Ambassador Sir Thomas Roe warn the East India Company NEVER to fight land wars or build fortresses in India?
parent_discussion.answer: Under Emperor Jahangir, the Mughal Empire was vastly wealthier and militarily stronger than Stuart England; English merchants survived only as polite petitioners.

parent_discussion.question: What had changed by 1765 that allowed Robert Clive to boast that a London business company had become "the sovereigns of a rich and potent kingdom"?
parent_discussion.answer: As central Mughal power weakened, the Company built private sepoy armies, bribed rival commanders like Mir Jafar at Plassey (1757), and seized Bengal’s tax system (the Diwani).

parent_discussion.question: Look closely at Clive’s final sentence: how did capturing Bengal’s taxes transform how the Company bought Indian textiles and Chinese tea?
parent_discussion.answer: Instead of shipping British silver to Asia to pay Indian weavers, the Company used Indian peasants’ own taxes to buy Indian goods for free—draining Bengal’s wealth and triggering the 1770 famine.

guided_reading.hinge_question:
Think: Compare Roe’s tone in 1616 with Clive’s tone in 1765—how many years separate the two extracts?

Pair: Why was winning the Diwani tax right in 1765 even more lucrative for the Company than looting a palace treasury once?

Share: Was the British conquest of Bengal planned from 1600, or opportunistic corporate imperialism?
questions: Where did Sir Thomas Roe tell the East India Company to seek its profit in 1616?
Which three provinces’ tax revenues passed to the East India Company under the 1765 Diwani?
Why did the Company no longer need to ship silver from England to buy Indian goods after 1765?
guided_reading.provenance_note: Original extracts from Ambassador Sir Thomas Roe’s 1616 Mughal court journal and Robert Clive’s 1765 Diwani letter, linked by brief context.

guided_reading.book_title: The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano: The Middle Passage (1789)
guided_reading.author: Olaudah Equiano (Chapter II, London, 1789 • British Library 615.d.11)
guided_reading.cover_caption: Abolitionist stowage diagram of the Liverpool slave ship Brookes under the Regulated Slave Trade Act of 1788, illustrating 454 enslaved men, women, and children packed below decks.
guided_reading.author_context: Olaudah Equiano (c. 1745–1797), known for much of his life as Gustavus Vassa, survived enslavement, purchased his own freedom in 1766 for forty pounds, and became a leading voice of the "Sons of Africa" abolitionist movement in London. Published in 1789 just as Parliament debated the slave trade, his bestselling autobiography shattered pro-slavery lies by placing eyewitness testimony of the Middle Passage directly into British readers’ hands.
guided_reading.extract:
"The first object which saluted my eyes when I arrived on the coast was the sea, and a slave ship, which was then riding at anchor, and waiting for its cargo. These filled me with astonishment, which was soon converted into terror when I was carried on board. I was immediately handled and tossed up to see if I were sound by some of the crew; and I was now persuaded that I had gotten into a world of bad spirits, and that they were going to kill me.

Soon after this the blacks who brought me on board went off, and left me abandoned to despair. I was soon put down under the decks, and there I received such a salutation in my nostrils as I had never experienced in my life: so that, with the loathsomeness of the stench, and crying together, I became so sick and low that I was not able to eat, nor had I the least desire to taste anything.

The closeness of the place, and the heat of the climate, added to the number in the ship, which was so crowded that each had scarcely room to turn himself, almost suffocated us. This produced copious perspirations, so that the air soon became unfit for respiration, from a variety of loathsome smells, and brought on a sickness among the slaves, of which many died—thus falling victims to the improvident avarice, as I may call it, of their purchasers. The shrieks of the women, and the groans of the dying, rendered the whole a scene of horror almost inconceivable."

vocabVault.def: The brutal six-to-twelve-week transatlantic sea voyage carrying enslaved Africans in chains from West Africa to the Americas.
A legal system treating enslaved human beings and their children as permanent private property ("cargo") to be bought and sold.
Extreme greed for financial profit—used by Equiano to expose slave traders’ motives.
The organised campaign by formerly enslaved writers, Black Britons, Quakers, and reformers to outlaw the slave trade and slavery.

parent_discussion.question: Why was Olaudah Equiano’s 1789 book far more powerful in changing British public opinion than dry parliamentary statistics alone?
parent_discussion.answer: Slave-ship owners claimed Africans were well treated on board; Equiano’s eloquent, first-hand account proved both the human agony below decks and the full intellectual equality of Black authors.

parent_discussion.question: Look at Equiano’s phrase "falling victims to the improvident avarice [short-sighted greed] of their purchasers": how does the Brookes ship diagram on the cover back up his words?
parent_discussion.answer: Merchants packed hundreds of people into spaces barely 2 feet 7 inches high to maximise profits, breeding suffocation and deadly epidemics.

parent_discussion.question: Which British ports grew wealthy building slave ships and trading slave-grown sugar, cotton, and tobacco between 1660 and 1807?
parent_discussion.answer: Liverpool, Bristol, and London financed thousands of triangular-trade voyages.

guided_reading.hinge_question:
Think: What happened to Equiano the moment he was carried onto the deck of the slave ship?

Pair: Cross-reference Equiano’s written description of conditions "under the decks" with the 1788 Brookes plan—how do text and diagram confirm one another?

Share: Why did Equiano address his book directly to the Members of both Houses of Parliament in 1789?
questions: What did the ship’s crew immediately do to Equiano when he was carried on board?
Why did the air below deck quickly become "unfit for respiration"?
What moral flaw in the slave traders ("purchasers") does Equiano blame for the deaths on board?
guided_reading.provenance_note: Original published text from Chapter II of Olaudah Equiano’s 1789 autobiography describing the Middle Passage.

guided_reading.book_title: The Jamaican Maroon Peace Treaty (1739) & Bryan Edwards on Maroon Guerrilla Warfare
guided_reading.author: Treaty of Cudjoe’s Town (1 March 1739 • CO 137/23) & Bryan Edwards (1796)
guided_reading.cover_caption: John Seller’s hand-coloured map of Jamaica (Insulae Jamaicae Descriptio), showing the rugged Blue Mountains and Cockpit Country interior where Maroon communities defied British armies.
guided_reading.author_context: Far from accepting plantation slavery passively, thousands of self-liberated Africans in Jamaica escaped into the limestone ravines of the Cockpit Country and the Blue Mountains. Led by brilliant tacticians Queen Nanny of the Windward Maroons and Captain Cudjoe of the Leeward Maroons, they defeated British redcoat regiments so decisively in the First Maroon War (1728–1739) that Colonial Governor Edward Trelawny had to sue for peace.
guided_reading.extract:
From planter-historian Bryan Edwards’s contemporary account of Maroon mountain tactics in The Proceedings of the Governor and Assembly of Jamaica (1796): "In the inaccessible fastnesses of the Cockpit Country—deep limestone glens flanked by precipices and tangled forest—European regular troops marched in scarlet coats only to be struck down by an unseen enemy. Communicating across miles of mountain peaks by the blast of the abeng [cow-horn trumpet] and camouflaged from head to foot in wild foliage, the Maroons ambushed British columns, cut off their baggage trains, and vanished before a single volley could be returned."

Forced to negotiate, Governor Edward Trelawny signed the Articles of Pacification with Captain Cudjoe on 1 March 1739 (followed by a treaty with the Windward Maroons in 1740):
"Article I: That all hostilities shall cease on both sides for ever.
Article II: That the said Captain Cudjoe, the rest of his Captains, Adherents, and Men, shall be for ever hereafter in a perfect state of freedom and liberty.
Article III: That they shall enjoy and possess, for themselves and their posterity for ever, all the lands situate and lying between Trelawny Town and the Cockpits, to the amount of fifteen hundred acres..."
Yet a painful colonial compromise followed in Article IX, requiring the Maroons to return future runaways from the sugar estates in exchange for crown recognition of their own freedom.

vocabVault.def: Communities of self-liberated Africans and their descendants who escaped Caribbean plantations and defended free mountain towns.
A curved cow-horn instrument blown by Jamaican Maroon lookouts to send coded messages across mountain valleys.
Hit-and-run ambush tactics using local terrain, speed, and camouflage to defeat a larger, heavily armed regular army.
The steep, jagged limestone mountain region of western Jamaica where Captain Cudjoe’s Leeward Maroons built unconquerable strongholds.

parent_discussion.question: Why were regular British soldiers in bright red uniforms repeatedly defeated by the Jamaican Maroons in the 1730s?
parent_discussion.answer: The Maroons knew every ravine of the Cockpit Country and Blue Mountains, used leaf camouflage, signalled across valleys with the abeng horn, and ambushed slow British columns.

parent_discussion.question: Why were Articles II and III of the 1739 Treaty such a historic victory nearly a century before Britain abolished slavery in 1833?
parent_discussion.answer: Almost a hundred years before emancipation, the mighty British Empire was forced in writing to recognise formerly enslaved Black leaders as free citizens owning 1,500 acres of land.

parent_discussion.question: Why do historians describe Article IX of the 1739 Treaty as a "tragic compromise"?
parent_discussion.answer: To secure peace and permanent legal freedom for their own mountain towns, Maroon leaders had to agree not to shelter newly escaped runaways from lowland sugar plantations.

guided_reading.hinge_question:
Think: What instrument did Maroon scouts use to communicate across mountain ridges?

Pair: Compare what the Maroons GAINED in Articles II–III with what the British planters DEMANDED in Article IX.

Share: How do Queen Nanny and Captain Cudjoe challenge the old myth that freedom was simply "gifted" from London?
questions: How did Maroon fighters disguise themselves and send signals across Jamaica’s mountains?
How many acres of land did Article III guarantee to Captain Cudjoe and his people?
What difficult condition did the British colonial government insert into Article IX of the 1739 treaty?
guided_reading.provenance_note: Original articles from the 1739 Jamaican Maroon Treaty paired with Bryan Edwards’s 1796 account and brief classroom context.

guided_reading.book_title: Declarations of the Stamp Act Congress (1765) & Eyewitness to the Boston Tea Party (1773)
guided_reading.author: Stamp Act Congress (19 Oct 1765) & George Robert Twelves Hewes (1773 Eyewitness)
guided_reading.cover_caption: William Bradford’s Pennsylvania Journal woodcut (31 October 1765), printing a skull and crossbones ("This is the Place to affix the STAMP") in protest against the British Stamp Act.
guided_reading.author_context: Victory in the Seven Years’ War (1756–1763) doubled Britain’s national debt to over £130 million. When Parliament taxed colonial newspapers and legal documents (1765 Stamp Act) and later granted the struggling East India Company a tea monopoly (1773 Tea Act), American colonists answered with constitutional protest and direct action—remembered vividly by Boston shoemaker George Robert Twelves Hewes.
guided_reading.extract:
From the Declaration of Rights and Grievances adopted by delegates of nine colonies at the Stamp Act Congress in New York (19 October 1765): "It is inseparably essential to the freedom of a people, and the undoubted right of Englishmen, that no taxes be imposed on them, but with their own consent, given personally, or by their representatives. That the people of these colonies are not, and from their local circumstances cannot be, represented in the House of Commons in Great Britain; that the only representatives of the people of these colonies are persons chosen therein by themselves."

Eight years later, on the freezing night of 16 December 1773, Boston shoemaker George Robert Twelves Hewes joined the "Sons of Liberty" boarding three East India Company ships moored at Griffin’s Wharf: "It was now evening, and I immediately dressed myself in the costume of an Indian, equipped with a small hatchet, and smeared my face and hands with coal dust in the shop of a blacksmith. When we arrived at the wharf, we were ordered by our commander to board the ships quietly and bring up all the chests of tea upon deck.

In about three hours from the time we went on board, we had broken and thrown overboard every tea chest to be found in the three ships—three hundred and forty-two chests in all—while strictly forbidding any man to steal a single ounce of tea or damage the ships’ rigging."

vocabVault.def: The colonial constitutional argument—rooted in Magna Carta and the 1689 Bill of Rights—that Westminster could not tax Americans who elected zero MPs.
Britain’s direct tax requiring paid revenue stamps on every colonial newspaper, legal contract, licence, and pack of playing cards.
Secret colonial protest networks of artisans, merchants, and dockworkers who organised boycotts and the 1773 Boston Tea Party.
Parliament’s harsh punishment after the Boston Tea Party—closing Boston Port and imposing military rule in Massachusetts.

parent_discussion.question: Notice how the 1765 Stamp Act Congress describes taxation by consent as "the undoubted right of Englishmen": where had the colonists learned that idea?
parent_discussion.answer: Directly from British history itself—Magna Carta (1215) and the English Bill of Rights (1689), which forbade taxing subjects without Parliament’s consent!

parent_discussion.question: Why did the Boston Tea Party protesters strictly forbid stealing tea for themselves or damaging any other part of the ships?
parent_discussion.answer: They wanted to prove to the world that the destruction of 342 East India Company tea chests was a disciplined political protest against unfair taxation, not a greedy riot.

parent_discussion.question: Look at how global the First British Empire had become by 1773: which company owned the tea dumped into Boston Harbor?
parent_discussion.answer: The British East India Company—connecting Mughal Bengal, London Parliament, and rebellious Boston in a single global web!

guided_reading.hinge_question:
Think: Why had Britain started taxing the Thirteen Colonies after 1763 in the first place?

Pair: Why did George III and Parliament think taxing colonists to pay for their own defence was fair, while colonists called it tyranny?

Share: How did Parliament’s furious reaction in 1774 turn a tax dispute into a war for independence?
questions: Why did the 1765 Stamp Act Congress say colonists could not be taxed by the House of Commons in London?
How many chests of East India Company tea were thrown into Boston Harbor on 16 December 1773?
What strict rule did the boarding parties enforce regarding stealing tea or damaging the ships?
guided_reading.provenance_note: Original 1765 Stamp Act Congress resolutions paired with shoemaker George Hewes’s eyewitness account of the 1773 Boston Tea Party.

guided_reading.book_title: Memoirs of the Life of Boston King: A Black Loyalist in the American Revolution (1798)
guided_reading.author: Boston King (published in The Methodist Magazine, London, March–June 1798)
guided_reading.cover_caption: John Trumbull, Surrender of Lord Cornwallis (1820, US Capitol Rotunda), depicting the October 1781 British defeat at Yorktown that decided American independence.
guided_reading.author_context: While Thomas Jefferson’s 1776 Declaration of Independence proclaimed that "all men are created equal," Jefferson himself enslaved over six hundred people. Tens of thousands of enslaved African Americans judged that liberty lay instead with British Emancipation proclamations (Lord Dunmore 1775; Philipsburg 1779). Carpenter and preacher Boston King (c. 1760–1802) escaped a South Carolina plantation to British lines, was registered in the 1783 Book of Negroes in New York, and published his gripping memoir in London in 1798.
guided_reading.extract:
"When the British troops took Charleston in South Carolina in 1780, word spread swiftly among the plantations that freedom was promised to all enslaved persons who reached the King’s lines. Resolving to risk death rather than remain in bondage, I borrowed a horse by night, slipped past the American patrols, and reached the British camp—where I was received as a free man, though smallpox soon swept fearfully through our tents.

Yet when peace was signed between Britain and the United States in 1783, unspeakable terror seized every Black Loyalist in New York. Rumours ran along the streets that all former slaves were to be delivered back to their old American masters, many of whom had already arrived in the city seizing people off the pavements! For days we could neither eat nor sleep for dread of returning to chains.

Mercifully, the British Commander-in-Chief, Sir Guy Carleton, stood firm by the Crown’s promise of freedom to all who had crossed into British lines for at least a year. My wife Violet and I had our names, ages, and former masters recorded in the great inspection ledger [the Book of Negroes], received our signed certificates of freedom, and set sail aboard HMS L’Abondance for Nova Scotia—and years later onward across the Atlantic to Freetown in Sierra Leone."

vocabVault.def: Roughly 20,000+ enslaved African Americans who escaped Rebel masters during the American Revolution to claim freedom behind British lines.
Virginia Royal Governor Lord Dunmore’s offer of freedom to enslaved people owned by Rebels if they joined British forces.
The official British military register recording 3,000 Black Loyalists evacuated as free people from New York to Nova Scotia, London, and the Caribbean.
The stark contradiction of Patriot leaders demanding freedom from British "slavery" while continuing to hold 500,000 Africans in chattel bondage.

parent_discussion.question: Why did enslaved people like Boston King and his wife Violet side with the British King rather than the American Patriots fighting for "liberty"?
parent_discussion.answer: American Patriot planters intended to keep slavery intact, whereas British commanders offered signed freedom certificates to enslaved people escaping Rebel estates.

parent_discussion.question: Why was peace in 1783 a moment of terror rather than celebration for Black Loyalists waiting in New York?
parent_discussion.answer: George Washington and American slaveholders demanded their escaped human "property" back; only British General Sir Guy Carleton’s refusal and the Book of Negroes saved 3,000 evacuees.

parent_discussion.question: Did Britain offer Dunmore’s Proclamation out of pure anti-slavery idealism, or military strategy?
parent_discussion.answer: Military strategy—Britain only freed enslaved people belonging to Rebel Patriots (while keeping slavery fully legal in loyal Jamaica and Barbados until 1833!).

guided_reading.hinge_question:
Think: What deadly disease struck Boston King soon after he reached the British camp?

Pair: Compare Thomas Jefferson’s words in 1776 ("all men are created equal") with Boston King’s real-life choices in 1780–1783.

Share: How did losing the Thirteen Colonies in 1783 push Britain eastward toward India and Australia?
questions: In which state and year did Boston King escape to the British army’s lines?
Why were Black Loyalists in New York terrified when peace was signed in 1783?
What official ledger recorded Boston and Violet King’s names before they sailed to Nova Scotia?
guided_reading.provenance_note: Condensed from Black Loyalist Boston King’s 1798 autobiography published in The Methodist Magazine, London.
