video.teacher_guidance: Recommended Watch Window: 00:00–03:33 | Lesson Phase: Lesson Hook | Tone Alert: Narrated by Terry Jones; engaging animated overview of the 1215 charter.
video.viewing_task:
[01:00] Quick Check: Where did King John meet the rebellious barons in June 1215 to seal Magna Carta?
[02:30] Hinge Question: Was Magna Carta a noble declaration of universal human freedom or a selfish protection pact for wealthy feudal barons?
video.model_answer:
Quick Check: Runnymede on the River Thames near Windsor.
Hinge Question: Originally, it was primarily a baronial peace treaty protecting aristocratic land, inheritances, and feudal privileges; however, Clauses 39 and 40 established the universal principle that no free man could be imprisoned without lawful trial.

video.title: Magna Carta | The Story of Britain | BBC Teach
video.teacher_guidance: Recommended Watch Window: 00:30–07:00 | Lesson Phase: Causal Breakdown | Tone Alert: Rigorous historical investigation into King John's failures in Normandy and tax extortion.
video.viewing_task:
[01:30] Recall: Why did King John lose Normandy ('John Lackland' / 'Softsword') to King Philip Augustus of France in 1204?
[03:45] Explain: How did John's extortionate 'scutage' taxes and mistreatment of baronial hostages provoke armed rebellion?
[06:00] Challenge: What is the enduring constitutional significance of Clause 39 ('No free man shall be seized or imprisoned... except by the lawful judgement of his equals')?
video.model_answer:
Recall: Military miscalculations, financial weakness, and the capture of Château Gaillard led to the loss of ancestral Norman lands.
Explain: John demanded exorbitant scutage (shield money) to fund failed French campaigns, seized estates, and imprisoned relatives of barons who failed to pay.
Challenge: Clause 39 established the bedrock of constitutional democracy: the monarch is subject to the rule of law, and the state cannot arbitrarily detain citizens without due process.

video.title: Ironclad (2011) | Official Movie Trailer (Paul Giamatti as King John)
video.teacher_guidance: Recommended Watch Window: 00:00–01:59 | Lesson Phase: Visual & Cultural Impact | Tone Alert: Gritty, visceral medieval drama depicting the 1215 Siege of Rochester Castle.
video.viewing_task: [01:10] Cinematic Discussion Focus: How does Paul Giamatti portray King John's fury at being forced to sign Magna Carta? How does the film depict the brutal reality of 13th-century siege warfare?
video.model_answer: Cinematic Discussion Focus: Giamatti portrays John as an enraged tyrant convinced of his divine right to rule unconditionally, viewing the barons as treasonous upstarts; the trailer captures the savage brutality of trebuchet bombardment and castle starvation.

video.title: The Legacy of Magna Carta & The Rule of Law | UK Parliamentary Archives
video.teacher_guidance: Recommended Watch Window: 00:00–03:53 | Lesson Phase: Flipped Learning / Extension | Tone Alert: Traces the influence of Magna Carta on the English Civil War, the US Constitution, and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
video.viewing_task:
[00:58] Recall: What happened within months of Runnymede when Pope Innocent III annulled Magna Carta at King John's request?
[01:56] Explain: How did the regency of the child king Henry III re-issue Magna Carta to save the Plantagenet dynasty?
[02:54] Challenge: How did 17th-century parliamentarians like Sir Edward Coke transform a medieval feudal charter into the foundation of parliamentary sovereignty?
video.model_answer:
Recall: The First Barons' War erupted; barons invited Prince Louis of France to invade England and claim the throne.
Explain: William Marshal reissued a modified charter in Henry III's name, reconciling the rebel barons and preserving the Crown.
Challenge: Coke used Magna Carta to challenge King Charles I's divine right in the 1628 Petition of Right, establishing that Parliament and the law were superior to the King's personal will.

video.title: BBC Two / ERA: History File – Medieval Realms, Ep. 3: Magna Carta (1215)
video.teacher_guidance: Recommended Watch Window: 01:00–14:30 | Lesson Phase: Baronial Rebellion & Runnymede | Tone Alert: BBC Two History File reconstructing why rebel barons forced King John to seal Magna Carta in 1215 and evaluating what the charter really meant for ordinary villeins.
video.viewing_task:
[03:00] Quick Check: Name two grievances—financial, military, or religious—that united the English barons in armed rebellion against King John by 1215.
[12:00] Hinge Question: Since most clauses of Magna Carta applied only to "free men" rather than unfree peasants (villeins), why is 1215 still remembered as a landmark in constitutional history?
video.model_answer:
Quick Check: Loss of Normandy in 1204, repeated heavy scutage taxes, arbitrary seizure of castles/hostages without trial, and the Papal Interdict closing English churches.
Hinge Question: Even though villeins were excluded at the time, Magna Carta established the revolutionary constitutional principle that the King himself was bound by the law and could not rule by whim alone.

sources.title: Source D: Magna Carta Parchment Exemplar: Clauses 39 and 40 (15 June 1215)
sources.caption: The 1215 Magna Carta (British Library Cotton MS Augustus II. 106). In Clause 39, John promises no free man shall be seized or stripped of property except by lawful judgement of his equals.
sources.author: Baronial Draftsmen and Royal Chancery Clerks
sources.question: Why do Clauses 39 and 40 of Magna Carta represent a revolutionary shift in the medieval concept of royal sovereignty?
sources.model_answer: Clauses 39 and 40 established for the first time that the monarch is subject to the law, not above it. By guaranteeing due process and forbidding the sale or denial of justice, Magna Carta transformed arbitrary royal extortion into a constitutional principle binding future crowns.

stages.title: Arrival of the Plague at Melcombe Regis
stages.trigger: In the summer of 1348, a merchant vessel docked at Melcombe Regis carrying bubonic plague, which spread rapidly across England and killed 35–50% of the population.
stages.connective: Decimated agricultural villages, emptied manors, and created an acute, unprecedented national labour shortage across the feudal countryside.
stages.question: How did the Black Death arrive in 1348 and spread across England?

stages.title: Labour Shortage & The Economic Revolution
stages.trigger: With fields left unploughed and crops rotting, surviving serfs and day-labourers discovered they could demand double wages or abandon their feudal manors.
stages.connective: Permanently weakened the economic grip of feudal landlords, giving ordinary peasants unprecedented bargaining power and social mobility.
stages.question: How did the shortage of farm workers give surviving peasants new power?

stages.title: The Statute of Labourers & Sumptuary Resistance
stages.trigger: Parliament passed the 1351 Statute of Labourers to freeze wages at pre-plague rates and enacted sumptuary laws to forbid peasants from wearing fine fabrics.
stages.connective: Provoked bitter generational class resentment among rural workers, who defied the wage caps and forged underground networks of mutual resistance.
stages.question: How did Parliament’s new laws of 1351 and 1363 anger working peasants?

stages.title: The Regressive Poll Taxes & Brentwood Spark
stages.actor: King Richard II, John Bampton & Essex Villagers
stages.trigger: To finance the costly Hundred Years’ War, Parliament imposed three regressive Poll Taxes, forcing impoverished peasants to pay the exact same twelve pence as wealthy lords.
stages.connective: Ignited armed insurrection when villagers drove royal tax collector John Bampton out of Brentwood, sparking a coordinated march on London.
stages.question: Why did the Poll Tax of 1381 spark an armed rebellion in Essex?

stages.title: Showdown at Smithfield & The End of Serfdom
stages.actor: Wat Tyler, Preacher John Ball & King Richard II
stages.trigger: Thousands of rebels stormed London, burning tax rolls and confronting fourteen-year-old King Richard II at Smithfield, where Wat Tyler was killed by the Mayor.
stages.connective: Although Richard revoked his promises of freedom, Parliament abandoned future Poll Taxes, and serfdom withered away over the next century.

narrative_blocks.title: Arrival of the Plague at Melcombe Regis (1348)
narrative_blocks.text: [5.1] In June 1348, the Black Death landed on English shores when a Sailor Ship at Weymouth (Melcombe Regis) carried plague-carrying fleas from Gascony. The pandemic spread with terrifying speed. Victims developed agonizing egg-sized black swelling Buboes Under the Arms and in the groin, spat dark blood, and suffered acute fever, perishing within three to five days. By 1350, with Nearly Half the Country Dead, entire villages lay deserted, churchyards overflowed into mass trenches, and medieval society stood shattered.
narrative_blocks.image_alt: Black Death Mass Burials
narrative_blocks.caption: Contemporary illustration of mass burials during the catastrophic Black Death of 1348–1350.
narrative_blocks.theme_heading: Demographic Catastrophe

sources.title: Source A: Chronicle of Henry Knighton on Plague Mortality and Labour Shortages (c. 1395)
sources.caption: Extract from Henry Knighton’s Chronicle (British Library Cotton MS Tiberius C. VII), recording catastrophic mortality, unharvested crops, and soaring wage demands following the 1348 plague.
sources.author: Henry Knighton, Augustinian Canon of St Mary de Pratis, Leicester
sources.citation: Henry Knighton, Chronicon Henrici Knighton (Leicester Abbey, c. 1395), British Library Cotton MS Tiberius C. VII.
sources.content: There was so great a scarcity of labour that many crops rotted in the fields for lack of harvesters, and cattle wandered untended through cornfields. In the autumn following, a reaper could not be hired for less than eightpence a day with his food, or a mower for less than twelvepence a day. Wherefore many crops perished in the fields for want of harvesters... But the labourers were so arrogant and obstinate that they took no heed of the King’s statute; if anyone wished to have them, he had to grant what they asked, and either lose his fruit and crops, or satisfy the lofty and covetous wishes of the workmen.
sources.question: According to Henry Knighton in Source A, how did the Black Death fundamentally disrupt the balance of power between lords and peasants?
sources.model_answer: Knighton explains that catastrophic mortality killed nearly half the workforce, leaving crops rotting in fields. Surviving agricultural labourers could demand double or triple wages, forcing desperate landlords to abandon feudal labour duties and pay cash to keep their estates solvent.
sources.context: In 1348–1350, the Black Death swept across England, killing an estimated 30–50% of the population and triggering a massive structural labour shortage.

The pandemic spread with terrifying speed. narrative_blocks.title: Labour Shortage & The Economic Revolution (1349–1351)
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.2] The catastrophic population collapse triggered an unprecedented economic revolution across the English countryside. Entire farming communities stood silent with empty village cottages, while overgrown fields were left abandoned with unharvested wheat rotting on the ground for lack of reapers.

For the first time in medieval history, surviving peasant labourers possessed immense economic bargaining power. Desperate landowners competed fiercely for workers, resulting in workers demanding double pay and boldly refusing unpaid feudal bondage, permanently shattering centuries of customary manorial control.

narrative_blocks.caption: Peasant labourers reaping wheat; after 1348, surviving workers demanded dramatically higher cash wages.
narrative_blocks.theme_heading: Socio-Economic Upheaval

sources.question: What does John Ball's sermon in Source C reveal about the revolutionary religious ideology behind the Peasants' Revolt?
sources.model_answer: Ball used biblical authority to argue that God created humanity as natural equals without kings, lords, or serfdom. By asking who was the 'gentleman' in the Garden of Eden, Ball provided a divine justification for dismantling feudal social hierarchy and overthrowing oppressive landlords.
sources.context: In June 1381, radical priest John Ball addressed over 30,000 peasant rebels at Blackheath outside London, urging them to cast off serfdom and demand total equality before the King.

narrative_blocks.title: The Statute of Labourers & Sumptuary Resistance (1351–1363)
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.3] Outraged by rising wages and their loss of feudal control, the landowner-dominated Parliament struck back decisively. The 1351 Statute of Labourers decreed that wages frozen by lords must remain strictly at pre-plague levels, making wage negotiation a punishable crime.

Runaway serfs faced imprisonment and having an iron "F" burned on foreheads for falsity to brand them as fugitive outlaws. Furthermore, 1363 Sumptuary Laws ensured commoners were banned from wearing fur, silk, or fine dyed cloth, entrenching bitter social resentment that exploded in rebellion thirty years later.
narrative_blocks.image_alt: Statute of Labourers 1351
narrative_blocks.caption: The parliamentary statute attempting to freeze peasant wages and enforce feudal servitude.
narrative_blocks.theme_heading: Feudal Retaliation & Repression

sources.question: What does Source D illustrate regarding the vulnerability of the English monarchy during the peak of the 1381 insurrection?
sources.model_answer: Source D shows the royal court physically isolated and trapped in the Tower of London while armed rebels controlled the capital. Richard II was forced to make sweeping promises—abolishing serfdom and granting general pardons—purely as a deceitful tactic to disperse the crowds until armed knights could regroup.
sources.context: On 14 June 1381, King Richard II rode out to Mile End to meet Wat Tyler, granting charter charters abolishing serfdom across England, which he later violently revoked.

[5.3] Outraged by rising wages and their loss of feudal control, the landowner-dominated Parliament struck back decisively. The 1351 Statute of Labourers decreed that wages frozen by lords must remain strictly at pre-plague levels, making wage negotiation a punishable crime.

Runaway serfs faced imprisonment and having an iron "F" burned on foreheads for falsity to brand them as fugitive outlaws. Furthermore, 1363 Sumptuary Laws ensured commoners were banned from wearing fur, silk, or fine dyed cloth, entrenching bitter social resentment that exploded in rebellion thirty years later.

narrative_blocks.title: The Regressive Poll Taxes & Brentwood Spark (1377–1381)
narrative_blocks.text: [5.4] Simmering tensions erupted when the royal government faced bankruptcy from the costly Hundred Years’ War, passing a crippling French War Debt Bill. Unlike property taxes, the third Poll Tax of 1381 demanded a flat Twelve Pence from Every Head aged over fifteen—equivalent to two weeks' hard wages for a labourer. Mass tax evasion followed, and when royal commissioner John Bampton arrived on 30 May 1381, he was a Tax Collector Chased with Pitchforks by furious Essex villagers at Brentwood, igniting armed rebellion.
narrative_blocks.image_alt: Medieval Froissart miniature of priest John Ball preaching from horseback in 1381
narrative_blocks.caption: Illuminated miniature from Jean Froissart’s Chronicles (c. 1470) showing radical priest John Ball ('Jehan Balle') preaching equality from horseback during the 1381 Peasants’ Revolt.
narrative_blocks.theme_heading: Fiscal Oppression & Revolt

sources.title: Source B: The Statute of Labourers (25 Edw. III, 1351): Parliamentary Cap on Agricultural Wages
sources.caption: Statute enacted by the English Parliament attempting to freeze agricultural and artisan wages at pre-plague 1346 levels and punishing runaway serfs with branding and imprisonment.
sources.author: King Edward III and the English Parliament
sources.content: Because a great part of the people, and especially of workmen and servants, late died of the pestilence, many seeing the necessity of masters, and great scarcity of servants, will not serve unless they may receive excessive wages... It is ordained, that every man and woman... shall be bounden to serve him which so shall him require, upon the wages accustomed... and if any workman or servant flee into another shire, he shall be taken and committed to gaol, and burned in the forehead with an iron formed to the letter F, in token of his falsity.
sources.question: Why did the 1351 Statute of Labourers create immense class bitterness that eventually exploded into the 1381 Peasants' Revolt?
sources.model_answer: Parliament was composed entirely of aristocratic and gentry landlords who used state legislation to artificially suppress wages and reassert serfdom. By criminalising peasants who sought fair market pay and branding runaway workers, the statute created three decades of seething resentment that boiled over in 1381.
sources.context: Following the Black Death, Edward III passed the Ordinance of Labourers (1349) and Parliament enacted the Statute of Labourers (1351) to prevent market wages from rising.
sources.hinge_question: Can any government law successfully stop the economic laws of supply and demand during an acute labour shortage?

narrative_blocks.title: Showdown at Smithfield & The End of Serfdom (1381)
narrative_blocks.text: [5.5] Under leaders Wat Tyler and radical priest John Ball, over 30,000 Peasants Swarm the Capital, burning tax rolls and storming the Tower of London. On 15 June 1381, fourteen-year-old King Richard II met the rebels at Smithfield. Tensions flared and Tyler Stabbed at the Peace Talks by the Mayor of London. With bows drawn, the bold Boy King Promises Freedom, declaring himself their leader and pledging to abolish serfdom. Though the revolt was brutally crushed, feudal bondage was terminally undermined and withered away over the next century.

narrative_blocks.caption: King Richard II confronting the rebel army at Smithfield after the death of Wat Tyler.

sources.caption: Illuminated miniature (British Library Royal MS 18 E. I, f. 175r): Lord Mayor William Walworth striking down rebel leader Wat Tyler before King Richard II at Smithfield on 15 June 1381.
sources.author: Flemish Illuminator for Froissart’s Chroniques
sources.question: How does the illumination in Source E reflect aristocratic relief and ideological bias against the lower-class rebels of 1381?
sources.model_answer: The illumination frames Tyler's murder as a righteous strike of civic defence by Lord Mayor Walworth, while Richard II bravely leads the bewildered crowd away. Once their charismatic leader was slain, the rebellion collapsed, allowing the Crown to execute over 1,500 rebels and reassert serfdom.
sources.context: On 15 June 1381, negotiations at Smithfield turned violent. Lord Mayor Walworth slashed Tyler, mortally wounding him and breaking the momentum of the revolt.

tasks.question: ‘The Black Death of 1348 was the main cause of the breakdown of the feudal system in medieval England.’ How far do you agree?
stimulus: The demographic collapse and labour shortage caused by the Black Death (1348–1350)
The 1351 Statute of Labourers and the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381
hints: Thesis / Introduction: State your criteria-led judgment on whether biological demographic shock (Black Death) or political resistance (1381 Peasants' Revolt) was more decisive [5.1, 5.5].
Arguments for Statement (Plague Impact): Explain how losing 40–50% of the population created an acute labour shortage, giving surviving serfs leverage for cash wages [5.1, 5.2].

Counter-Arguments (Rebellion & Legislation): Explain how Parliament attempted to freeze wages via the 1351 Statute of Labourers, and how the 1381 revolt against poll taxes broke landlord resolve [5.3–5.5].
Sustained Judgement: Conclude whether the plague created the irreversible economic conditions while the 1381 rebellion dealt the political death blow to serfdom [5.1–5.5].
tasks.starter: It can be argued that the Black Death was the main cause of the breakdown of the feudal system because... However, an alternative view is that...
tasks.gold_challenge: Historian Challenge: Weigh the long-term demographic and economic impact of the Black Death against the immediate political impact of the 1381 Peasants’ Revolt in destroying serfdom.

quick_quiz.question: In what year did the Black Death arrive in England aboard a ship from Gascony?
quick_quiz.q: In what year did the Black Death arrive in England aboard a ship from Gascony?
quick_quiz.explanation: The Black Death docked at Melcombe Regis in Dorset in the summer of 1348.

quick_quiz.question: At which Dorset port did the ship carrying the Black Death first dock in England?
quick_quiz.q: At which Dorset port did the ship carrying the Black Death first dock in England?
quick_quiz.explanation: The lethal pestilence entered England through the port of Melcombe Regis (modern Weymouth) in Dorset.

quick_quiz.question: What bacterium caused the Black Death epidemic in medieval Europe?
quick_quiz.q: What bacterium caused the Black Death epidemic in medieval Europe?
quick_quiz.explanation: Modern science identified Yersinia pestis, carried by rat fleas, as the causative plague organism.

quick_quiz.question: What visible physical symptom gave the bubonic plague its distinctive name?
quick_quiz.q: What visible physical symptom gave the bubonic plague its distinctive name?
options: Agonizing black swellings (buboes) in the groin and armpits
A red ring-shaped rash across the chest
quick_quiz.answer: Agonizing black swellings (buboes) in the groin and armpits
quick_quiz.a: Agonizing black swellings (buboes) in the groin and armpits
quick_quiz.explanation: Victims developed agonizing swellings called buboes in the groin and armpits before spitting blood.

quick_quiz.question: What proportion of England's entire population is estimated to have perished during the Black Death by 1350?
quick_quiz.q: What proportion of England's entire population is estimated to have perished during the Black Death by 1350?
quick_quiz.explanation: Between one-third and one-half of England's total population died within barely eighteen months.

quick_quiz.question: Why did surviving agricultural labourers gain sudden economic bargaining power after the Black Death?
quick_quiz.q: Why did surviving agricultural labourers gain sudden economic bargaining power after the Black Death?
options: A severe labour shortage meant landlords were desperate for workers to harvest crops
Peasants purchased all manor houses from impoverished lords
The King granted all farm workers royal knighthoods
The Church gave all tithes directly to agricultural labourers
quick_quiz.answer: A severe labour shortage meant landlords were desperate for workers to harvest crops
quick_quiz.a: A severe labour shortage meant landlords were desperate for workers to harvest crops
quick_quiz.explanation: With half the labour force dead, basic laws of supply and demand allowed surviving peasants to demand higher wages.

quick_quiz.question: What parliamentary law was passed in 1351 to freeze wages and prevent peasants from changing employers?
quick_quiz.q: What parliamentary law was passed in 1351 to freeze wages and prevent peasants from changing employers?
quick_quiz.explanation: Parliament passed the Statute of Labourers in 1351, making it illegal to pay or receive higher wages.

quick_quiz.question: At what year's wage rates did the 1351 Statute of Labourers attempt to freeze agricultural wages?
quick_quiz.q: At what year's wage rates did the 1351 Statute of Labourers attempt to freeze agricultural wages?
quick_quiz.explanation: The statute demanded that wages remain frozen at the pre-plague rates of 1346.

quick_quiz.question: What physical punishment was prescribed for labourers who repeatedly demanded higher pay under the 1351 statute?
quick_quiz.q: What physical punishment was prescribed for labourers who repeatedly demanded higher pay under the 1351 statute?
options: Being branded on the forehead with the letter 'F' (for Falsity)
quick_quiz.answer: Being branded on the forehead with the letter 'F' (for Falsity)
quick_quiz.a: Being branded on the forehead with the letter 'F' (for Falsity)
quick_quiz.explanation: Disobedient workers could be branded on the forehead with a hot iron with the letter 'F'.

quick_quiz.question: Which young king reigned over England during the outbreak of the Peasants' Revolt in 1381?
quick_quiz.q: Which young king reigned over England during the outbreak of the Peasants' Revolt in 1381?
quick_quiz.explanation: Fourteen-year-old Richard II sat on the throne when the Peasants' Revolt erupted in 1381.

quick_quiz.question: What form of taxation provoked the outbreak of the Peasants' Revolt in 1381?
quick_quiz.q: What form of taxation provoked the outbreak of the Peasants' Revolt in 1381?
quick_quiz.explanation: Parliament levied three crushing Poll Taxes between 1377 and 1381 to fund the Hundred Years' War.

quick_quiz.question: How much was demanded from every individual over age fifteen under the 1381 Poll Tax?
quick_quiz.q: How much was demanded from every individual over age fifteen under the 1381 Poll Tax?
quick_quiz.explanation: The 1381 poll tax demanded 12 pence (one shilling) from everyone over fifteen—two weeks' wages.

quick_quiz.question: In which Essex town were royal tax commissioners attacked with bows and arrows on 30 May 1381?
quick_quiz.q: In which Essex town were royal tax commissioners attacked with bows and arrows on 30 May 1381?
quick_quiz.explanation: Villagers in Brentwood defied tax collector John Bampton, sparking open rebellion across Essex.

quick_quiz.question: Who was the experienced soldier from Kent who emerged as the primary military leader of the rebels?
quick_quiz.q: Who was the experienced soldier from Kent who emerged as the primary military leader of the rebels?
quick_quiz.explanation: Wat Tyler led the Kentish rebels, marching them into London to confront the King.

quick_quiz.question: Which radical priest inspired the revolt with the sermon: 'When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?'?
quick_quiz.q: Which radical priest inspired the revolt with the sermon: 'When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?'?
quick_quiz.explanation: Radical priest John Ball preached against feudal inequality, questioning hereditary nobility.

quick_quiz.question: Approximately how many armed peasants marched on London in June 1381?
quick_quiz.q: Approximately how many armed peasants marched on London in June 1381?
quick_quiz.explanation: Over 30,000 rebels from Essex and Kent converged upon the capital in June 1381.

quick_quiz.question: Which magnificent palace belonging to John of Gaunt was burned to the ground by rebels in London?
quick_quiz.q: Which magnificent palace belonging to John of Gaunt was burned to the ground by rebels in London?
quick_quiz.explanation: The rebels destroyed the luxurious Savoy Palace on the Strand, throwing John of Gaunt's wealth into the Thames.

quick_quiz.question: Where did King Richard II meet Wat Tyler for open negotiations on 15 June 1381?
quick_quiz.q: Where did King Richard II meet Wat Tyler for open negotiations on 15 June 1381?
quick_quiz.explanation: The young King agreed to meet Wat Tyler in the open fields of Smithfield outside London's walls.

quick_quiz.question: Who struck and fatally wounded Wat Tyler during the confrontation at Smithfield?
quick_quiz.q: Who struck and fatally wounded Wat Tyler during the confrontation at Smithfield?
options: William Walworth, the Mayor of London
quick_quiz.answer: William Walworth, the Mayor of London
quick_quiz.a: William Walworth, the Mayor of London
quick_quiz.explanation: Mayor William Walworth drew his blade and wounded Tyler after an altercation with the royal party.

quick_quiz.question: What long-term impact did the Peasants' Revolt have on English society despite the execution of its leaders?
quick_quiz.q: What long-term impact did the Peasants' Revolt have on English society despite the execution of its leaders?
options: Parliament never levied another poll tax and serfdom died out completely within a century
The monarchy was abolished and a republic declared
Feudalism was legally reinforced for another 300 years
All taxation was permanently ended across England
quick_quiz.answer: Parliament never levied another poll tax and serfdom died out completely within a century
quick_quiz.a: Parliament never levied another poll tax and serfdom died out completely within a century
quick_quiz.explanation: Parliament never dared pass another poll tax, and economic reality led to the total demise of serfdom.

flashcards.definition: A 1351 law attempting to freeze wages at pre-plague rates and punish mobile workers.
A regressive flat tax levied equally on every individual person regardless of income.
The hereditary legal bondage of peasants tied to a lord’s manorial estate.

lessons.prologue: In the summer of 1348, a terrifying pestilence arrived on merchant ships from Europe, wiping out nearly half of England's population within two years. When surviving farmworkers demanded higher wages, landlords clamped down with harsh poll taxes. In 1381, peasant rebels marched on London with scythes and banners. How did plague and rebellion shatter medieval feudalism?

sources.title: Source A: Chronicle of Henry Knighton on Plague Mortality and Labour Shortages (c. 1395)
sources.caption: Extract from Henry Knighton’s Chronicle (British Library Cotton MS Tiberius C. VII), recording catastrophic mortality, unharvested crops, and soaring wage demands following the 1348 plague.
sources.author: Henry Knighton, Augustinian Canon of St Mary de Pratis, Leicester
sources.citation: Henry Knighton, Chronicon Henrici Knighton (Leicester Abbey, c. 1395), British Library Cotton MS Tiberius C. VII.
sources.content: There was so great a scarcity of labour that many crops rotted in the fields for lack of harvesters, and cattle wandered untended through cornfields. In the autumn following, a reaper could not be hired for less than eightpence a day with his food, or a mower for less than twelvepence a day. Wherefore many crops perished in the fields for want of harvesters... But the labourers were so arrogant and obstinate that they took no heed of the King’s statute; if anyone wished to have them, he had to grant what they asked, and either lose his fruit and crops, or satisfy the lofty and covetous wishes of the workmen.
sources.question: According to Henry Knighton in Source A, how did the Black Death fundamentally disrupt the balance of power between lords and peasants?
sources.model_answer: Knighton explains that catastrophic mortality killed nearly half the workforce, leaving crops rotting in fields. Surviving agricultural labourers could demand double or triple wages, forcing desperate landlords to abandon feudal labour duties and pay cash to keep their estates solvent.

sources.question: What does John Ball's sermon in Source C reveal about the revolutionary religious ideology behind the Peasants' Revolt?
sources.model_answer: Ball used biblical authority to argue that God created humanity as natural equals without kings, lords, or serfdom. By asking who was the 'gentleman' in the Garden of Eden, Ball provided a divine justification for dismantling feudal social hierarchy and overthrowing oppressive landlords.

sources.question: What does Source D illustrate regarding the vulnerability of the English monarchy during the peak of the 1381 insurrection?
sources.model_answer: Source D shows the royal court physically isolated and trapped in the Tower of London while armed rebels controlled the capital. Richard II was forced to make sweeping promises—abolishing serfdom and granting general pardons—purely as a deceitful tactic to disperse the crowds until armed knights could regroup.

sources.question: How does the illumination in Source E reflect aristocratic relief and ideological bias against the lower-class rebels of 1381?

Once their charismatic leader was slain, the rebellion collapsed, allowing the Crown to execute over 1,500 rebels and reassert serfdom.

lessons.vocab_cloze_text: England’s [Demography] changed dramatically after the Black Death of 1348–49 killed over a third of the population and created acute labour shortages. Angry lords passed the 1351 [Statute of Labourers] to freeze wages and preserve [Serfdom]. When King Richard II’s government collected three unfair [Poll Tax] levies by 1381, Wat Tyler and John Ball led a dramatic peasant [Insurrection] into London.

key_individuals.name: King Edward the Confessor
key_individuals.role: Last King of the House of Wessex (1042–1066)
key_individuals.origins: Pious Anglo-Saxon monarch who reigned for twenty-four years and rebuilt Westminster Abbey, yet died childless on 5 January 1066 with no direct blood heir.
key_individuals.significance: His childless death plunged Northwestern Europe into the 1066 succession crisis, leaving the Anglo-Saxon Witan to elect Harold Godwinson while Duke William of Normandy and King Harald Hardrada of Norway prepared rival invasions.
achievements: Allegedly promised the English crown to his cousin Duke William of Normandy in 1051 before naming Earl Harold Godwinson protector of the realm on his deathbed.
Buried in Westminster Abbey in January 1066, within twenty-four hours of which the Witan crowned Harold II.

key_individuals.name: King Harold II (Harold Godwinson)
key_individuals.role: Earl of Wessex & Last Crowned Anglo-Saxon King of England (1066)
key_individuals.origins: England’s wealthiest nobleman and Earl of Wessex, elected king by the Witan in January 1066 despite Norman claims that he had sworn a sacred 1064 oath on holy relics supporting Duke William.
key_individuals.significance: Marched 190 miles north in four days to annihilate Harald Hardrada’s Vikings at Stamford Bridge (25 September 1066), before force-marching 250 miles south to die defending Senlac Hill at Hastings on 14 October 1066.
achievements: Crushed Harald Hardrada’s 300-longship Viking invasion at Stamford Bridge on 25 September 1066, leaving only 24 ships needed for the survivors.
Held Senlac Hill near Hastings for five hours behind an interlocking shield wall of elite housecarls and fyrd militia until Norman feigned retreats broke the line and Harold was killed.

key_individuals.name: King Harald Hardrada
key_individuals.role: King of Norway & Viking Claimant to the English Throne (1046–1066)
key_individuals.origins: Fearsome Norwegian warrior-king ("Hard-Ruler") who claimed the English crown through an earlier pact between Scandinavian rulers and sailed 300 Viking longships to Yorkshire in September 1066.
key_individuals.significance: Forced King Harold II to march his elite housecarls 190 miles north just days before Duke William landed at Pevensey—fatally exhausting England’s army even though Hardrada himself was killed at Stamford Bridge.
achievements: Landed 300 Viking longships on the Yorkshire coast in September 1066.
Killed by an arrow to the throat during King Harold’s surprise assault at the Battle of Stamford Bridge (25 September 1066), ending the Viking Age in England.

key_individuals.name: William the Conqueror (Duke William of Normandy)
key_individuals.role: Duke of Normandy & First Norman King of England (1066–1087)
key_individuals.origins: Formidable Duke of Normandy who secured the papal banner of Pope Alexander II, landed unopposed at Pevensey Bay in late September 1066, and defeated Harold II at Hastings using disciplined cavalry feigned retreats.
key_individuals.significance: Subjugated two million Anglo-Saxons with an elite of ten thousand Normans through 500 rapid motte-and-bailey castles, the merciless 1069–70 Harrying of the North, total feudal land redistribution, and the 1086 Domesday Book.
achievements: Won the Battle of Hastings (14 October 1066) by tipping back his helmet to rally panicking troops and ordering feigned cavalry retreats to shatter the Saxon shield wall.
Built over 500 timber motte-and-bailey castles (later stone keeps such as Portchester) and unleashed the Harrying of the North (1069–70), recorded by Orderic Vitalis as starving over 100,000 people.
Commissioned the 1086 Domesday Book survey across every English shire, replacing Anglo-Saxon thegns with ~200 Norman barons bound by feudal knight service.

key_individuals.name: King Henry II
key_individuals.role: First Plantagenet King of England & Ruler of the Angevin Empire (1154–1189)
key_individuals.origins: Energetic Angevin ruler determined to restore royal law and order across England—including ending the scandal of "criminous clerks" escaping royal gallows in lenient Church courts by reading a Latin verse ("benefit of clergy").
key_individuals.significance: Appointed his close friend and Chancellor Thomas Becket as Archbishop of Canterbury in 1162 expecting a loyal ally, issued the 1164 Constitutions of Clarendon, and suffered European outrage and barefoot public penance (1174) after his furious outburst prompted four knights to murder Becket.
achievements: Issued the Constitutions of Clarendon (January 1164) demanding that defrocked criminal clerics face punishment in royal courts.
His angry Christmas 1170 outburst spurred four royal knights to murder Archbishop Becket in Canterbury Cathedral on 29 December 1170.
Walked barefoot through Canterbury in July 1174 to be whipped with birch rods by eighty monks at Becket’s shrine, conceding clerical court immunity.

key_individuals.name: Archbishop Thomas Becket
key_individuals.role: Royal Chancellor (1155–62), Archbishop of Canterbury & Canonised Martyr
key_individuals.origins: Once Henry II’s wealthy hunting companion in silk robes, Becket shocked the court upon becoming Archbishop of Canterbury in June 1162 by resigning the Chancellorship, wearing a lice-infested goat hairshirt, and declaring loyalty solely to the Pope.
key_individuals.significance: Refused to seal the 1164 Constitutions of Clarendon, spent six years in French exile, and was hacked down at the altar of Canterbury Cathedral on 29 December 1170—becoming medieval England’s greatest martyr-saint and forcing Henry II to back down over Church courts.
achievements: Defended independent Church courts ("benefit of clergy") against royal jurisdiction at Clarendon (1164) and excommunicated bishops who backed the King in December 1170.
Martyred in Canterbury Cathedral on 29 December 1170 and canonised by Pope Alexander III within three years, turning Canterbury into a major European pilgrimage shrine.

key_individuals.name: King John
key_individuals.role: Plantagenet King of England Sealed at Runnymede (1199–1216)
key_individuals.origins: Younger brother of Richard the Lionheart who lost ancestral Normandy to King Philip II of France in 1204 (earning the nickname "John Softsword") and spent a decade squeezing heavy feudal taxes and scutage from English barons.
key_individuals.significance: Provoked a five-year Papal Interdict (1208–13), saw his continental coalition crushed at Bouvines (1214), and—cornered after rebel barons led by Robert Fitzwalter seized London—affixed the Great Seal to Magna Carta at Runnymede on 15 June 1215.
achievements: Clashed with Pope Innocent III over Archbishop Stephen Langton, enduring the 1208 Interdict and 1209 excommunication before surrendering England as a papal fief in 1213.
Sealed the 63 clauses of Magna Carta at Runnymede on 15 June 1215—including Clause 39 guaranteeing free men lawful judgement by equals and the law of the land.

Persuaded the Pope to annul Magna Carta within months, sparking the First Barons’ War (and losing crown baggage in the Wash) before dying in October 1216, when William Marshal reissued the Charter for nine-year-old Henry III.

key_individuals.name: Pope Innocent III
key_individuals.role: Head of the Medieval Catholic Church (1198–1216)
key_individuals.origins: Most powerful medieval Pope, who asserted supreme spiritual authority over European monarchs from Rome.
key_individuals.significance: Demonstrated the immense religious power of the medieval papacy by placing all England under a five-year Interdict (1208) and excommunicating King John (1209) until John knelt as a papal vassal—after which Innocent annulled Magna Carta in 1215.
achievements: Locked English church doors for five years under the 1208 Interdict when King John rejected Stephen Langton as Archbishop of Canterbury.
Accepted England as a tribute-paying papal fiefdom in 1213, then declared Magna Carta shameful, illegal, and void at John’s request in August 1215.

key_individuals.name: John Ball & Wat Tyler
key_individuals.lifespan: Ball: c. 1338 – July 1381 · Tyler: d. 15 June 1381
key_individuals.role: Radical Preacher & Military Leader of the 1381 Peasants’ Revolt
key_individuals.origins: Following the 1348–50 Black Death, the wage-freezing 1351 Statute of Labourers, and the flat 12-pence third Poll Tax of May 1381 (sparked when Essex villagers chased tax commissioner John Bampton from Brentwood), Kentish rebel Wat Tyler freed radical priest John Ball.
key_individuals.significance: Led over 30,000 Essex and Kent rebels into London in June 1381—burning tax rolls, storming the Tower of London, and preaching human equality ("When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?")—accelerating the long-term collapse of English serfdom.
achievements: John Ball preached radical Christian equality to massed rebels at Blackheath outside London.
Wat Tyler presented demands to abolish serfdom and cap land rents to King Richard II before being stabbed by London’s Mayor at Smithfield on 15 June 1381.

key_individuals.name: King Richard II
key_individuals.role: Fourteen-Year-Old Boy King During the 1381 Peasants’ Revolt (1377–1399)
key_individuals.origins: Fourteen-year-old grandson of Edward III whose royal ministers imposed three regressive Poll Taxes (culminating in 12d per adult in 1381) to pay French war debts from the Hundred Years’ War.
key_individuals.significance: Displayed cool nerve at Mile End and Smithfield on 14–15 June 1381—riding forward when Wat Tyler was killed ("I shall be your captain!") to disperse the rebel army with promises of freedom, before revoking every charter and executing rebel leaders.
achievements: Promised charters abolishing serfdom to disperse armed rebels at Mile End and Smithfield (June 1381).

Revoked his freedom charters once royal forces regrouped ("Villeins ye are, and villeins ye shall remain"), though labour shortages after the Black Death meant feudal bondage steadily withered away anyway.

guided_reading.book_title: Gesta Guillelmi (The Deeds of William): Senlac Hill & the Feigned Retreat
guided_reading.author: William of Poitiers (c. 1071 • Norman Court Chronicle)
guided_reading.cover_caption: Scene from the Bayeux Tapestry (c. 1070s) showing mounted Norman knights charging the locked kite-shields and battleaxes of King Harold’s English huscarls.
guided_reading.author_context: William of Poitiers (c. 1020–1090) was a Norman chaplain who had trained as a knight before entering the Church and serving Duke William of Normandy. Writing around five years after 1066, his Latin chronicle Gesta Guillelmi flatters his Norman patron, yet provides our most detailed military account of how Norman cavalry broke the English shield-wall on 14 October 1066.
guided_reading.extract:
"The English stood massed tightly upon the crest of the hill, holding the high ground in so dense a wedge that the dead could scarcely fall where they stood. Hurling javelins and wielding terrible two-handed battleaxes that clove through shields and coats of mail alike, King Harold’s warriors drove back our foot-soldiers and Bretons upon the left wing.

When false cries arose among the ranks that Duke William himself had fallen, flight began to spread across the valley. Seeing the peril, the Duke spurred his charger across the path of the retreating knights, pushed back his iron helmet so that every man might behold his bare face, and cried aloud: 'Look at me well! I live, and by God’s grace I shall conquer! What madness drives you to flee when victory lies before you?'

Perceiving thereafter that the tightly locked English shield-wall could not be shattered by headlong assault uphill, the Normans twice turned their horses in deliberate, feigned flight. Drawn down from their ridge in eager pursuit of what seemed a beaten enemy, thousands of the English broke formation on the lower slope—whereupon our horsemen wheeled swiftly round, surrounded the scattered pursuers, and cut them down."

vocabVault.def: A tightly locked defensive formation in which Anglo-Saxon huscarls and fyrdmen overlapped shields on high ground.
Elite, salaried professional bodyguards of the Anglo-Saxon king who fought with heavy mail and two-handed Danish axes.
A disciplined cavalry tactic of pretending to flee in panic in order to lure defenders out of a strong defensive position.
Support and reward given by a powerful ruler to a writer or churchman, often shaping how chronicles praise that ruler.

parent_discussion.question: Why was it almost impossible for Duke William’s soldiers to break the English army during the morning of 14 October 1066?
parent_discussion.answer: Harold’s army held the steep top of Senlac Hill in a tightly locked shield-wall, where Norman horses struggled uphill against two-handed battleaxes.

parent_discussion.question: How did Duke William stop his army panicking when a rumour spread that he had been killed, and how did the feigned retreat work?
parent_discussion.answer: He lifted his helmet to show his face alive, then used pretended retreats to trick English fighters into chasing downhill and breaking their shield-wall.

parent_discussion.question: Knowing that William of Poitiers was Duke William’s own chaplain, why should historians read his praise of Norman cleverness carefully?
parent_discussion.answer: As a Norman court chronicler writing for the Conqueror, he exaggerates William’s genius while downplaying how exhausted Harold’s troops already were after marching south from Stamford Bridge.

guided_reading.hinge_question:
Think: What weapon did the English huscarls use that terrified William’s knights?

Pair: Compare this chronicle with Scene 55 of the Bayeux Tapestry—how do both sources corroborate William lifting his helmet?

Share: Was Hastings won more by Norman tactics or English exhaustion after Stamford Bridge?
questions: Why could the English soldiers on the hilltop "scarcely fall where they stood"?
What did Duke William do with his helmet to prove to his retreating troops that he was still alive?
How did the Norman "feigned flight" trick the English defenders into losing their advantage?
guided_reading.provenance_note: Translated from Latin and condensed for KS3 reading aloud from William of Poitiers’s c. 1071 Norman chronicle.

guided_reading.book_title: Historia Ecclesiastica: Orderic Vitalis on Castles & the Harrying of the North
guided_reading.author: Orderic Vitalis (Book IV, c. 1125 • Monastery of Saint-Évroul)
guided_reading.cover_caption: Bayeux Tapestry scene inscribed "ISTE IVSSIT VT FODERETVR CASTELLVM AT HESTENGACEASTRA", showing forced English labourers digging the motte-and-bailey castle at Hastings.
guided_reading.author_context: Orderic Vitalis (1075–c. 1142) was born in Shropshire to a Norman father and an English mother before becoming a Benedictine monk in Normandy. Because of his mixed Anglo-Norman heritage, Orderic wrote with rare moral honesty—praising King William’s strength while fiercely condemning the merciless starvation inflicted on Yorkshire during the Harrying of the North (1069–1070).
guided_reading.extract:
"Throughout the conquered shires the King planted royal castles—earthworks crowned with timber palisades that the English had scarcely known before, which prevented the people of the land from rising cleanly against his garrisons. Yet when the men of Northumbria joined Danish raiders at York in 1069, King William’s wrath knew no restraint.

Nowhere else had William shown such cruelty. Yielding to his anger, he spared neither the weak nor the innocent, commanding that all crops, herds of cattle, ploughs, and stores of grain between York and Durham be burned to ashes so that rebels might find no winter sustenance.

From that deliberate ruin so dreadful a famine swept across northern England that defenceless men, women, and children perished of hunger upon the frozen roads—more than one hundred thousand Christian souls, as men reckoned. Though I have often praised King William’s vigour and order, I dare not excuse so brutal a slaughter; for surely Almighty God, the righteous Judge, will weigh the cries of the starving alongside the deeds of princes."

vocabVault.def: A Norman fortress combining a raised earthen mound (motte) topped by a wooden keep with a fenced courtyard (bailey) below.
Systematic scorched-earth devastation—burning crops, livestock, and villages to starve a region into submission.
A body of armed knights and soldiers stationed inside a castle to control the surrounding countryside.
Bringing a conquered population completely under royal obedience through force, law, and taxation.

parent_discussion.question: Why were Norman motte-and-bailey castles such a shock and threat to Anglo-Saxon communities?
parent_discussion.answer: England had very few private castles before 1066; towering earthen mottes and mounted garrisons allowed small numbers of Normans to dominate whole shires.

parent_discussion.question: Why did King William burn ploughs, barns, and cattle across Yorkshire in the winter of 1069–1070 rather than simply fighting rebel soldiers?
parent_discussion.answer: By destroying food supplies and tools ("scorched earth"), he ensured no northern rebellion or Danish army could feed itself—causing catastrophic famine for civilians.

parent_discussion.question: Why does Orderic Vitalis’s mixed English and Norman background make his verdict on William so valuable to historians?
parent_discussion.answer: Even though he lived in a Norman monastery and admired William’s order, his English roots made him refuse to whitewash the starvation of innocent northern families.

guided_reading.hinge_question:
Think: What triggered William’s fury in northern England in 1069?

Pair: Note Orderic’s figure of "100,000" dead—why did medieval chroniclers use huge round numbers, and how does the 1086 Domesday Book ("wasteland" / vasta) prove the devastation really happened?

Share: Which did more to secure Norman control permanently: castles, terror, or Domesday taxation?
questions: What new type of fortification did King William build across the English shires?
What items did William order his troops to burn between York and Durham in 1069–1070?
Why does Orderic Vitalis say he "dare not excuse" William’s actions in the North?
guided_reading.provenance_note: Translated from Latin and condensed for KS3 pupils from Orderic Vitalis’s c. 1125 monastic chronicle.

guided_reading.book_title: Vita Sancti Thomae: Eyewitness Account of the Murder in the Cathedral
guided_reading.author: Edward Grim (c. 1172 • British Library Cotton MS Claudius B II)
guided_reading.cover_caption: Historical engraving of King Henry II kneeling barefoot in penance before the tomb of St Thomas Becket at Canterbury Cathedral in July 1174.
guided_reading.author_context: Edward Grim was a clerk from Cambridge visiting Archbishop Thomas Becket at Canterbury on the evening of 29 December 1170. When four household knights of King Henry II—Reginald FitzUrse, Hugh de Morville, William de Tracy, and Richard le Breton—stormed into the cathedral, Grim stood beside Becket and had his own arm nearly severed by the first sword blow before writing this famous eyewitness biography.
guided_reading.extract:
"As twilight fell on the twenty-ninth of December, the monks hurried Archbishop Thomas toward the cathedral vespers, begging him to bolt the heavy oak doors behind them. Turning calmly upon the steps, Thomas forbade them: 'It is not right to turn the fortress of prayer, the Church of Christ, into a military camp. Even if it stands unlocked, it is able to shield its own; we shall triumph over our foes by suffering rather than by fighting.'

Moments later the four mailed knights burst in with drawn swords and axes, shouting aloud: 'Where is Thomas Becket, traitor to the King and the realm?' Receiving no answer, they cried again, 'Where is the Archbishop?' At once Thomas stepped down from the pillar into plain view and answered clearly: 'Here I am—no traitor to the King, but a priest of God. What do you seek?'

When they demanded that he lift the excommunication placed upon the King’s bishops, Thomas refused unless they submitted to the authority of the Church. Though I threw my own arm forward to turn aside the first descending blade—whereby my arm was grievously cut—the Archbishop bowed his head in prayer, commending his cause to God and St Denis, and fell beneath their swords upon the stone pavement."

vocabVault.def: The most senior churchman in England, responsible for leading the English Church under the Pope in Rome.
Officially expelling a person from the Catholic Church and its sacraments—a terrifying spiritual punishment in medieval Europe.
A person killed because they refuse to surrender their religious faith or principles.
A public act of sorrow and punishment carried out to seek God’s forgiveness for a grave sin.

parent_discussion.question: Why did Archbishop Thomas Becket refuse to let the terrified monks lock the doors of Canterbury Cathedral?
parent_discussion.answer: He insisted a church is a house of prayer, not a castle, believing sacred sanctuary should never be barred to anyone.

parent_discussion.question: What was the core argument between King Henry II and Becket that led the four knights to confront him?
parent_discussion.answer: Who held supreme authority over Church courts and bishops in England—the Crown (Constitutions of Clarendon) or the Church and Pope.

parent_discussion.question: How did murdering Becket inside Canterbury Cathedral completely backfire on King Henry II?
parent_discussion.answer: Christendom was horrified; Becket was swiftly declared a saint and martyr, forcing Henry II to walk barefoot through Canterbury to be whipped in penance in 1174 and compromise on Church courts.

guided_reading.hinge_question:
Think: Why is Edward Grim such an extraordinary eyewitness source for 29 December 1170?

Pair: At the same time, Grim wrote to celebrate Becket as a saint—which details in his account emphasize Becket’s saintly bravery?

Share: Who won the struggle between Crown and Church after 1170: Henry II or Becket?
questions: Why did Thomas Becket order the monks not to bolt the cathedral doors?
What accusation did the four knights shout when they entered Canterbury Cathedral?
How was eyewitness author Edward Grim injured during the attack?
guided_reading.provenance_note: Translated from Latin and abridged for KS3 reading aloud from eyewitness Edward Grim’s c. 1172 account at Canterbury.

guided_reading.book_title: Flores Historiarum & Magna Carta: Confrontation at Runnymede (June 1215)
guided_reading.author: Roger of Wendover (St Albans Chronicle, c. 1235) & Magna Carta Clauses 12, 39 & 61
guided_reading.cover_caption: Historical engraving depicting King John seated in his pavilion at Runnymede beside the River Thames surrounded by mailed rebel barons and bishops in June 1215.
guided_reading.author_context: Roger of Wendover (died 1236) was the chronicler of St Albans Abbey, a great monastery just north of London through which royal officials and rebel barons constantly passed. Paired here with the translated Latin text of the Great Charter sealed at Runnymede on 15 June 1215, his account captures how military defeat in France and crushing scutage taxes forced King John to accept the rule of law.
guided_reading.extract:
Roger of Wendover records how England’s barons renounced their fealty in the spring of 1215 after years of arbitrary fines, lost wars in Normandy, and heavy scutage taxes: "Gathering an army styling itself the Army of God and Holy Church, the barons marched upon London, whose citizens opened the city gates to them. Seeing himself deserted by almost all his knights save a handful of foreign mercenaries, King John met the barons in the water-meadow called Runnymede, between Windsor and Staines, on the fifteenth day of June."

There the King’s Great Seal was pressed into wax beneath the clauses of Magna Carta:
"Clause 12: No scutage or aid shall be imposed in our kingdom unless by the common counsel of our kingdom..."
"Clause 39: No free man shall be seized or imprisoned, or stripped of his rights or possessions, or outlawed or exiled, nor will we proceed with force against him, except by the lawful judgment of his equals or by the law of the land."
"Clause 40: To no one will we sell, to no one deny or delay right or justice."
"Clause 61: The barons shall choose any twenty-five barons of the kingdom to observe, hold, and cause to be observed the peace and liberties which we have granted."

vocabVault.def: "Shield money"—a feudal tax demanded by King John instead of military service, which he levied eleven times to fund failed wars.
In 1215, landowners, knights, barons, and townsmen who were not unfree peasant villeins tied to a lord’s manor.
The constitutional principle that even the monarch must obey the law rather than ruling by personal whim.
The water-meadow beside the River Thames near Windsor where King John agreed to Magna Carta on 15 June 1215.

parent_discussion.question: Why had England’s barons grown furious enough with King John to capture London in 1215?
parent_discussion.answer: John had lost Normandy to France, demanded repeated scutage taxes, seized barons’ castles and hostages without trial, and quarrelled with the Pope.

parent_discussion.question: Why did Clauses 39 and 40 not immediately give rights to everyone living in England in 1215?
parent_discussion.answer: Clause 39 applied only to "free men" (barons, knights, and freemen), leaving out the majority of English peasants who were unfree villeins.

parent_discussion.question: Even if the barons in 1215 mainly wanted to protect their own wealth (plus Clause 61’s committee of 25 barons), why did Magna Carta become world-famous?
parent_discussion.answer: It established in writing that the king is beneath the law, cannot imprison people without fair trial, and cannot tax the realm without common consent.

guided_reading.hinge_question:
Think: Which event forced King John to negotiate at Runnymede in June 1215?

Pair: Look closely at Clause 39 and Clause 61: which clause lasted for 800 years, and which clause caused civil war within months?

Share: Was Magna Carta a timeless charter of human liberty or a feudal barons’ power grab?
questions: Which city opened its gates to the rebel barons, leaving King John isolated in 1215?
According to Clause 39, who was protected against imprisonment without lawful judgment?
How many barons did Clause 61 appoint to watch over King John and enforce the charter?
guided_reading.provenance_note: Combines translated clauses of Magna Carta (1215) with Roger of Wendover’s St Albans chronicle account.

guided_reading.book_title: Historia Anglicana: John Ball’s Blackheath Sermon & the 1381 Rising
guided_reading.author: Thomas Walsingham (St Albans Abbey Chronicle, c. 1381–1394)
guided_reading.cover_caption: Illuminated detail from Jean Froissart’s Chronicles inscribed "Iehā Balle", depicting radical priest John Ball preaching from horseback during the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381.
guided_reading.author_context: After the Black Death (1348–1349) killed between a third and half of England’s population, surviving peasants realised their labour was scarce—yet lords enforced the 1351 Statute of Labourers to freeze wages and imposed three flat-rate Poll Taxes between 1377 and 1381. Monastic chronicler Thomas Walsingham of St Albans disliked the rebels intensely, yet preserved the revolutionary words preached by radical priest John Ball at Blackheath on 12 June 1381.
guided_reading.extract:
"After the Commons of Kent and Essex had broken open Maidstone gaol and freed the priest John Ball, a vast multitude of country folk gathered upon Blackheath overlooking London. Taking for his text the rhyme that had passed secretly from village to village, John Ball preached thus to the throng:

'When Adam delved [dug] and Eve span [spun wool], who was then the gentleman? From the beginning all human beings were created equal by nature; bondage and serfdom were brought in not by God’s will, but by the unjust oppression of wicked men! Now is the hour given to you by God, if you have the courage, to cast off the heavy yoke of villeinage that you have borne so long, and win the liberty you have always desired.'

Stirred by his words and enraged by the collectors of the third Poll Tax, the rebels marched under Wat Tyler across London Bridge, burned the legal manor rolls that recorded their unfree birth, and demanded of fourteen-year-old King Richard II at Mile End that no man in England should henceforth be a serf."

vocabVault.def: Unfree feudal status tying peasants to their lord’s manor, requiring unpaid week-work and fines for permission to marry or move.
The hated flat-rate "head tax" of 1381 in which a poor farm labourer had to pay the exact same twelve pence (three groats) as a wealthy lord.
Written parchment court records held by lords that proved which families owed unfree feudal labour.
The medieval hierarchy exchanging land for loyalty, knight-service, and peasant labour.

parent_discussion.question: What did John Ball mean by his famous question, "When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?"
parent_discussion.answer: In the biblical Garden of Eden there were no lords or serfs—so class inequality and serfdom were invented by human greed, not ordained by God.

parent_discussion.question: How were the Black Death of 1348 and the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381 directly connected?
parent_discussion.answer: The plague created a severe shortage of workers; when Parliament blocked rising wages (1351 Statute of Labourers) and added unfair Poll Taxes, emboldened peasants rebelled.

parent_discussion.question: Why did the rebels in 1381 deliberately target and burn parchment manor rolls rather than looting randomly?
parent_discussion.answer: Burning the written legal records of villeinage showed they had clear political goals: erasing proof of unfree serfdom so they could rent land freely for cash wages.

guided_reading.hinge_question:
Think: Why was the 1381 Poll Tax considered far more unfair than normal taxes?

Pair: Thomas Walsingham was a wealthy abbey chronicler whose own monastery owned serfs—how might that bias his attitude toward Wat Tyler and John Ball?

Share: Even though Wat Tyler and John Ball were killed in 1381, why had serfdom largely disappeared across England within seventy years?
questions: Which prison did the Kent rebels break open to free the priest John Ball?
Quote the famous opening rhyme of John Ball’s sermon at Blackheath.
Which specific documents did the rebels burn to destroy proof of their unfree status?
guided_reading.provenance_note: Translated and condensed for KS3 reading aloud from Thomas Walsingham’s chronicle of the 1381 Peasants’ Revolt.

data.synopsis: Crowns shattered, royal heads rolling from the executioner's block, and an island kingdom consumed by religious fury and civil war. From the spark of Henry VIII’s seismic Break with Rome and the deadly religious pendulum of the Tudor monarchs to the gunpowder treason of 1605 and the fiery sea battle against the Spanish Armada. Witness Charles I claim absolute Divine Right, triggering a bloody clash between Royalist Cavaliers and Cromwell's New Model Army that culminated in public regicide, the puritan Republic, and the revolutionary birth of constitutional monarchy in the Glorious Revolution of 1689.
data.title: Crown, Church, or Parliament (1517–1689)
data.enquiry: Who had the right to rule Britain: King, Church, or Parliament?
data.description: From the spark of the Protestant Reformation and Henry VIII’s Break with Rome to the execution of Charles I and the 1689 Bill of Rights, explore how 170 years of religious conflict, civil war, and constitutional struggle transformed Britain from an absolute monarchy into a parliamentary state.

glossary.definition: A 16th-century religious movement that challenged the Catholic Church and created Protestant churches.
A certificate sold by the Catholic Church promising forgiveness of sins and less time in Purgatory.
The 1534 law that made the English monarch the Supreme Head of the Church of England instead of the Pope.
The rapid, dizzying religious swings in England between Edward VI (radical Protestant) and Mary I (strict Catholic).
Elizabeth I’s 1559 compromise: a Protestant national church that retained traditional ceremonies to avoid religious rebellion.
Being officially cast out of the Catholic Church by the Pope, declaring a ruler to be a heretic.
A massive fleet of warships sent by Philip II of Spain in 1588 to invade England and restore Catholicism.
The belief that a monarch’s authority comes directly from God and that no parliament or court can question them.
An ancient coastal tax that Charles I illegally forced inland towns to pay during his 11-year Personal Rule.
Oliver Cromwell’s disciplined, professional Parliamentary army, promoted by military ability rather than aristocratic birth.
The deliberate execution or murder of a reigning monarch (such as King Charles I in January 1649).
The 1689 constitutional law guaranteeing that monarchs cannot suspend laws, levy taxes, or keep an army without Parliament.

stages.title: The Dynastic Succession Crisis
stages.trigger: Catherine of Aragon failed to produce a surviving male heir, convincing Henry that their marriage was cursed by God and threatening England with dynastic civil war.
stages.connective: Propelled Henry to demand a papal annulment and fall passionately in love with Anne Boleyn, setting the Crown on a collision course with Rome.
stages.question: Why did King Henry desperately want a royal annulment by 1527?

stages.title: Roman Deadlock & Papal Imprisonment
stages.actor: Pope Clement VII & Emperor Charles V
stages.trigger: Emperor Charles V’s imperial troops sacked Rome and held Pope Clement VII captive, preventing the Pope from insulting the Emperor by annulling his aunt Catherine’s marriage.
stages.connective: Paralyzed English diplomacy, destroyed Cardinal Wolsey’s career, and convinced Henry that foreign popes must not control English domestic affairs.
stages.question: Why did Pope Clement VII refuse to end Henry’s marriage to Catherine?

stages.title: Cromwell’s Parliamentary Squeeze
stages.trigger: Thomas Cromwell drafted parliamentary statutes that banned financial payments to Rome and declared England an autonomous empire subject to no foreign jurisdiction.
stages.connective: Stripped the English clergy of papal protection, validated Henry’s secret marriage to Anne Boleyn, and legally severed England from Rome.
stages.question: How did Thomas Cromwell use Parliament to break Rome’s power by 1533?

stages.title: The Act of Supremacy & Royal Sovereignty
stages.trigger: Parliament passed the 1534 Act of Supremacy, declaring the King to be the only Supreme Head on Earth of the Church of England, enforced by lethal Treason oaths.
stages.connective: Completed the constitutional revolution, ending 1,000 years of papal jurisdiction and transferring immense monastic wealth to the Crown.
stages.question: How did the 1534 Act of Supremacy increase King Henry’s power and wealth?

lessons.did_you_know: Young Henry VIII was an athletic, vain prince who wrote love letters and bad poetry to Anne Boleyn. Terrified of bad smells and the sweating sickness, he carried a hollow pomander ball filled with perfumed spices everywhere, and wore custom-padded shoes wider than they were long to look colossal!

items.question: In medieval Catholic churches, what vivid wall painting warned worshippers who could not read about Heaven and Hell?
items.explanation: Painted above the chancel arch, Doom paintings reminded medieval Christians of the Last Judgment.

items.question: In what language were Catholic church services, prayers, and the Bible written across Western Europe before the 1500s?
items.explanation: Ordinary parishioners could not read the Latin Bible for themselves and relied on priests to interpret Scripture.

items.question: Who was the supreme spiritual head of the Western Catholic Church, governing Christendom from Rome?
items.explanation: Before the 1500s, English monarchs and bishops recognised the spiritual authority of the Pope in Rome.

items.question: What 10% annual religious tax did every medieval farming household have to pay to the Church from their produce?
items.explanation: Villagers gave one-tenth of their grain, wool, and livestock every year to support the parish priest and Church.

items.question: From whom did medieval European monarchs claim they received their ultimate authority to rule?
items.explanation: Anointed with holy oil at their coronation, medieval monarchs claimed God had chosen them to govern.

items.question: Who conquered England in October 1066 after defeating King Harold II at the Battle of Hastings?
items.answer: William the Conqueror (Duke William of Normandy)
items.explanation: William's Norman Conquest reshaped England's monarchy, castles, cathedrals, and landowning aristocracy.

items.question: Which Archbishop of Canterbury was murdered inside his cathedral in 1170 during a fierce dispute with King Henry II?
items.explanation: Becket's murder showed how bitterly English kings and the Catholic Church could clash over legal authority.

items.question: Which famous charter of 1215 forced King John to accept that even the monarch was subject to the law of the land?
items.explanation: Sealed at Runnymede in 1215, Magna Carta restricted arbitrary royal taxation and unlawful imprisonment.

items.question: What were the wealthy religious houses where medieval Catholic monks and nuns lived, prayed, and farmed vast estates?
items.explanation: Hundreds of monasteries owned roughly a quarter of England's land before the sixteenth century.

items.question: Which royal dynasty took the English crown in 1485 at the end of the Wars of the Roses?
items.explanation: Henry VII founded the Tudor dynasty in 1485, determined to prevent England sliding back into civil war over succession.

items.question: Which 15th-century European invention allowed books and pamphlets to be copied rapidly instead of written out by hand?
items.explanation: Movable-type printing presses enabled new religious and political arguments to spread across Europe within weeks.

items.question: What assembly of noble Lords and elected local representatives was summoned by English monarchs to approve taxes and laws?
items.explanation: Evolving since the thirteenth century, Parliament held growing authority over national taxation and statute law.

lessons.prologue: In 1527, King Henry VIII faced a desperate crisis: his queen had produced no surviving male heir. When the Pope refused to annul the marriage, Henry struck back. He severed ties with Rome, seized England’s wealthy monasteries, and declared himself Supreme Head. Was this break driven by faith, or by power and dynastic survival?

narrative_blocks.title: The Spark at Wittenberg (1517–1521)
narrative_blocks.text:
[1.1] In October 1517, German monk Martin Luther nailed 95 fiery arguments to the Wittenberg church door. Luther attacked corrupt friars selling an indulgence—a certificate promising that paying for forgiveness would free dead relatives from the agonies of Purgatory.

Printed copies spread across Europe, triggering the Protestant Reformation. When young King Henry VIII wrote a book defending Catholic sacraments against Luther, Pope Leo X rewarded him with the proud Defender of the Faith title.

source.title: Source A (Theological Schism): Martin Luther in Academic Doctor's Robes (Lucas Cranach the Elder, 1529)
source.caption: Oil on panel by Lucas Cranach the Elder (1529, Uffizi Gallery / St. Anne's Museum) depicting Martin Luther in dignified academic doctor's gown and scholar's beret, gazing steadfastly forward as the intellectual catalyst of European Protestantism.
source.author: Lucas Cranach the Elder
source.question: How does Cranach's portrait present Martin Luther as a courageous scholar-theologian rather than a rebellious heretic?
source.model_answer: Cranach depicts Luther wearing dignified, high-collared academic doctor's robes and a scholar's cap, gazing steadfastly ahead with a solemn expression. This portrays him not as an anarchic outlaw or heretic, but as an authoritative Doctor of Theology standing firm on biblical scholarship against corrupt papal indulgences.
source.context: In October 1517, Martin Luther attacked papal corruption by circulating his 95 Theses in Wittenberg, sparking the Protestant Reformation across Europe.
source.hinge_question: Why was the invention of printing crucial for turning Luther's local protest into an unstoppable European revolution?

narrative_blocks.title: The King’s Dynastic Crisis (1525–1527)
narrative_blocks.text:
[1.2] By 1527, Henry faced an agonizing dynastic crisis. Catherine of Aragon was past forty and had borne only one living daughter, Princess Mary. Driven by a desperate need for a son to protect royal succession, Henry feared civil war if the Tudor dynasty collapsed without a male heir.

Having fallen deeply in love for Anne Boleyn, Henry cited a strict Bible warning on marriage from Leviticus, claiming his marriage to Catherine was cursed. He demanded an official papal annulment to marry again.

source.title: Source B (Dynastic Propaganda): The Family of Henry VIII: An Allegory of the Tudor Succession (c. 1545)
source.caption: Allegorical dynastic painting (Royal Collection Trust) showing Henry VIII flanked by Jane Seymour and Prince Edward, with Mary and Philip (war) on the left and Elizabeth with Peace and Plenty on the right.
source.author: English Court School Painter
source.question: What does Source B reveal about why King Henry VIII was obsessed with securing a male heir?
source.model_answer: The painting places young Prince Edward at the absolute centre alongside Henry and the deceased Jane Seymour. This demonstrates Henry's conviction that only a male Tudor heir could guarantee dynastic legitimacy and prevent England from descending into renewed civil war.
source.context: Henry VIII's desperate quest for a legitimate male heir led him to seek the annulment of his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, triggering the Break with Rome.

items.title: Catherine of Aragon
items.takeaway: When the Pope refused to end this marriage, Henry broke away from Rome to marry again.

items.title: Anne Boleyn
items.takeaway: Backed English Bibles and the Break with Rome, but was executed on treason charges after failing to bear a son.

items.title: Jane Seymour
items.takeaway: Gave Henry his longed-for male heir, future King Edward VI, before dying twelve days after childbirth.

items.title: Anne of Cleves
items.takeaway: Arranged by Thomas Cromwell as a German alliance; Henry ended the marriage quickly and executed Cromwell.

items.title: Catherine Howard
items.takeaway: Teenage cousin of Anne Boleyn backed by Catholic nobles; executed for treasonous adultery in 1542.

items.title: Catherine Parr
items.takeaway: Reunited Henry with daughters Mary and Elizabeth and raised young Prince Edward as a Protestant.

narrative_blocks.title: The Roman Deadlock (1527–1529)
narrative_blocks.text:
[1.3] Normally, popes readily granted royal annulments, but Pope Clement VII was trapped. In May 1527, Holy Roman Emperor Charles V—Catherine’s nephew—led imperial troops that attacks Rome, ransacked the city, and left the Pope held prisoner in Castel Sant’Angelo.

Charles warned the papacy that ending Catherine’s marriage would bring ruin. When Henry’s chief minister Cardinal Wolsey opened a legatine court in London, Clement revoked the case, the church trial cancelled, and English sovereignty was defied, causing Wolsey’s immediate arrest.
narrative_blocks.image_alt: Contemporary oil painting of Cardinal Thomas Wolsey, Lord Chancellor to King Henry VIII
narrative_blocks.caption: Cardinal Thomas Wolsey (c. 1473–1530), Lord Chancellor and Archbishop of York, charged by Henry VIII with securing the papal annulment from Pope Clement VII (National Portrait Gallery, London / NPG 320).

source.title: Source C (Monarchical Supremacy): Portrait of King Henry VIII (Hans Holbein the Younger, c. 1537)
source.caption: Monumental royal portrait by Hans Holbein the Younger (Walker Art Gallery, Liverpool), projecting absolute monarchical majesty, physical bulk, and sovereign defiance.
source.author: Hans Holbein the Younger
source.question: How does Holbein use posture and imperial symbolism to convey Henry VIII's supreme royal authority over both Church and State?
source.model_answer: Holbein paints Henry frontally with legs braced apart, opulent jewel-encrusted robes, and hands grasping a dagger and gloves. This imposing stance projects unyielding power, communicating that Henry acknowledged no earthly or papal superior over the English kingdom.
source.context: Following the Break with Rome, Henry used royal portraiture to project supreme imperium, styling himself as an Old Testament king and Supreme Head of the Church.
source.hinge_question: How did Holbein's visual propaganda help establish the concept of the 'Imperial Crown' of England?
